DISCUSSION  The tumor immune microenvironment remains a formidable barrier to effective immunotherapy, particularly in solid tumors characterized by dense myeloid infiltration (  3  ,   4  ). Among these, neutrophils have emerged as highly plastic yet underappreciated regulators of tumor progression (  5  ,   6  ). Our study provides evidence that CAP, a non-pharmacological and locoregionally deliverable modality, can functionally reprogram TANs and thereby reinvigorate antitumor immunity. By integrating in vitro and in vivo therapeutic studies across both syngeneic and humanized tumor models, we demonstrate that CAP acts through a mitochondria-centered mechanism to shift neutrophils from an immunosuppressive state toward cytotoxic and immunostimulatory phenotype.  The heterogeneity of neutrophils in cancer has posed a significant challenge in understanding their dualistic roles in tumor immunity (  3  ,   4  ,   6  ). Our spatial transcriptomic and single-cell analyses revealed distinct phenotypic profiles between neutrophils in NMIBC versus MIBC. Neutrophils in MIBC exhibited a transcriptional signature consistent with immunosuppression and metabolic quiescence. These findings underscore the functional diversity of TANs and reveal their potential contribution to immunotherapy resistance, particularly in tumors marked by T cell exclusion and high neutrophil burden.  Previous efforts to modulate neutrophil function in cancer have largely focused on systemic depletion using CXCR2 antagonists or anti-Ly6G antibodies, or on blockade of neutrophil recruitment through chemokine targeting (  41  ,   42  ). Notably, in contrast to depletion-based or recruitment-blocking strategies that aim to eliminate neutrophils systemically, CAP strategy emphasizes functional re-education of tumor-associated neutrophils in situ, preserving their host-protective capacity while redirecting their activity toward tumor control. More recent strategies have attempted to polarize neutrophils toward antitumor states using pharmacologic agents such as IFN-β, TGF-β inhibitors, or nanocarrier-based cytokine delivery (  10  –  12  ). However, such approaches are limited by transient effects, systemic toxicity, and poor spatiotemporal control (  43  ). In contrast, our study establishes a drug-free, locoregionally applicable strategy that leverages physical modulation of immune cell metabolism to reprogram tumor-associated neutrophils in situ. By exploiting the unique redox sensitivity of neutrophils, CAP circumvents the need for systemic manipulation and offers a tunable, clinically compatible platform for overcoming myeloid-driven immunosuppression. Several lines of evidence indicate that CAP differs from classical pharmacological neutrophil stimuli in both mode and duration of activation, supporting its potential as a biophysical approach to modulate neutrophil function within the tumor microenvironment.  In vivo, localized CAP treatment markedly reduced bladder tumor burden and prolonged survival in orthotopic models, with minimal systemic toxicity. The antitumor effect was dependent on the presence of neutrophils, as genetic ablation of these cells abrogated CAP efficacy. Interestingly, while CAP did not significantly alter neutrophil abundance in the tumor, it profoundly reshaped their activation state, consistent with a functional reprogramming rather than trafficking-based mechanism. This distinction is crucial, as most previous attempts to target TANs have relied on systemic depletion or trafficking inhibition, approaches that lack precision and carry risk of immune compromise.  The translational potential of this approach is supported by our studies in a humanized patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model, which demonstrated robust tumor inhibition and enhanced CD8 +  T cell function without notable systemic toxicity. The intravesical delivery method employed here mimics clinical administration routes in bladder cancer, providing a feasible path toward first-in-human studies. Given the broad presence of neutrophil-rich, immune-cold phenotypes in many solid tumors, including lung, pancreatic, and colorectal cancers, CAP may offer a generalized strategy for myeloid reprogramming across multiple malignancies.  Nevertheless, this study has several limitations. While we demonstrate clear evidence of mitophagy inhibition and oxidative activation in neutrophils following CAP exposure, the upstream molecular sensors and signaling pathways mediating this response warrant further investigation. Moreover, although our murine and humanized models recapitulate key aspects of the human immune-tumor interface, clinical validation in patients is required to fully assess safety, durability, and efficacy. Future studies should also explore the kinetics of CAP-induced reprogramming, potential effects on other stromal populations, and combinatorial regimens beyond PD-1 blockade. Although our data support CAP-mediated restoration of TANs cytotoxic activity and partial alleviation of T cell-suppressive features, the current study cannot yet fully determine the extent to which these effects reflect direct immunosuppression reprogramming of TANs in vivo. Further studies will be required to better define the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms.  In conclusion, our findings define a drug-free strategy to reprogram tumor-associated neutrophils through physical modulation of mitochondrial dynamics. By shifting neutrophils toward a cytotoxic, immunostimulatory state, CAP restores both innate and adaptive immune responses and enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint therapy. This work provides a mechanistic framework and preclinical rationale for harnessing biophysical interventions to overcome myeloid-driven immune resistance in cancer ( Fig. 7D ).    MATERIALS AND METHODS   Mice  Female C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (RRID: MGI:2159769). Ly6G-DTR transgenic mice (C57BL/6 background) and  Rag1 −/−   mice (C57BL/6 background) were obtained from Cyagen Biosciences. Humanized hu-HSC-NOG-EXL mice (10 weeks after hematopoietic stem cell engraftment) were purchased from Charles River Laboratories. All animals were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions with controlled temperature and humidity on a 12-hour light/dark cycle. All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Qilu Hospital of Shandong University (Approval No. KYLL-202402-016-1).  Orthotopic bladder tumors were established in 8–10-week-old female immunocompetent mice by intravesical instillation of 5 × 10 5  bladder cancer cells under isoflurane anesthesia using aseptic technique. Neutrophil-depleted conditions were generated in parallel experiments using Ly6G-DTR mice treated with diphtheria toxin (DT; Calbiochem, #322326) at 20 μg/kg via intraperitoneal injection every 72 hours to maintain sustained neutrophil ablation. Tumor growth was monitored longitudinally by bioluminescence imaging following intraperitoneal administration of D-luciferin (150 mg/kg) under isoflurane anesthesia using an IVIS Lumina system (PerkinElmer). Tumor burden was further assessed by high-resolution transabdominal ultrasonography (Vevo LAZR, VisualSonics) following bladder distension with PBS via catheterization.  For therapeutic studies, mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups using a random number generator. Transvesical CAP treatment and/or intraperitoneal anti–PD-1 antibody (10 mg/kg) were administered on alternating three-day schedules as indicated. Body weight was recorded throughout the study, and bladder tumors were harvested at experimental endpoints for histological and molecular analyses. Sample sizes (5–10 mice per group) were determined based on prior experience with orthotopic bladder tumor models and published literature; no formal power calculation was performed. No predefined exclusion criteria were applied. No animals were excluded from analysis unless technical failure occurred. Investigators were not blinded during treatment administration; however, tumor measurements and histological analyses were performed in a blinded manner. Mice were monitored daily, and humane endpoints were applied if tumor burden exceeded ethical limits or animals exhibited signs of distress.    Patients  Bladder cancer patients undergoing radical cystectomy or transurethral resection at Qilu Hospital of Shandong University were prospectively enrolled in this study. Whole blood samples and tumor tissues were collected for neutrophil isolation. The study cohort included adult patients (age range 57–86 years; 12 males and 3 females). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to sample collection. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Qilu Hospital of Shandong University (Approval Nos. KYLL-202409-052-1 and KYLL-202402-016-1) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Information on ethnicity was not systematically collected.    Cell lines  The mouse bladder carcinoma cell line MB49 (C57BL/6 origin; RRID: CVCL_7076) was obtained from Millipore. The human bladder carcinoma cell line T24 (ATCC Cat# HTB-4; RRID: CVCL_0554) and the human uroepithelial cell line SV-HUC-1 (ATCC Cat# CRL-9520; RRID: CVCL_3798) were purchased from ATCC. MB49 cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% (v/v) penicillin–streptomycin. T24 and SV-HUC-1 cells were cultured according to ATCC recommendations in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. All cell lines were maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . All cell lines were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination and were confirmed to be negative. Cells were used at low passage numbers after thawing and were not cultured beyond 20 passages.    Xenium 5 k Experiment and Analyzer

CAP equipment and treatment  The plasma jet device used in this study consists of two coaxial quartz glass tubes and two metal electrodes, enabling a double-layer dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) configuration. A high-voltage rod-shaped electrode (diameter: 3 mm) is enclosed by the inner quartz tube (outer diameter: 4 mm, inner diameter: 3 mm). The outer quartz tube is fitted with a nozzle at its lower end (outer diameter: 6 mm, inner diameter: 5 mm). A copper coil, wrapped around the exterior of the nozzle, serves as the ground electrode. The distance between the two electrodes is 6 mm, with the ground electrode positioned 6 mm from the nozzle outlet. To prevent direct contact with the working gas and avoid arcing with the high-voltage electrode, the ground electrode is enclosed within a plastic protective cover. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) was generated using a high-voltage power supply delivering 15 kV at a frequency of 5 kHz. Argon (99.99%) was used as the working gas at a flow rate of 72 liter hour −1 .  For in vitro assay, culture medium was exposed directly to CAP for indicated time, then cells were treated with CAP-activated medium for further analysis. Considering that CAP treatment exhibited the biological effects through reactive species, this study used a constant discharge power and lengthened the treatment time to increase the content of reactive species in different CAP treatment groups. To better describe the dose of CAP, the preset time was used to visually define the actual treatment dose of the CAP treatment (table S1).  For in vivo experiments, a custom-built CAP sprayer was used to treat tumor-bearing mice. This sprayer shares a similar double-layer DBD structure, comprising two coaxial quartz tubes and two metal electrodes. A high-voltage rod electrode (diameter: 0.75 mm) is positioned inside the inner quartz tube (outer diameter: 2 mm, inner diameter: 1 mm), while the outer tube (outer diameter: 4 mm, inner diameter: 3 mm) is equipped with a nozzle (outer diameter: 3 mm, inner diameter: 2 mm) at its bottom end. Plasma is generated through a flexible PTFE catheter (length: 30 mm, inner diameter: 0.6 mm, outer diameter: 0.9 mm). The ground electrode, a copper coil, is wound around the exterior of the nozzle, and the distance between the high-voltage electrode tip and the ground electrode is 6 mm. Operational parameters included an argon gas flow rate of 18 liter hour −1  per tube and a discharge voltage of 15 kV at 1 kHz. Tumor-bearing mice were sequentially treated with the plasma jet, with each session lasting 15 minutes. During the experiment, the plasma sprayer system could be arranged in an array configuration for broader treatment coverage (table S1).    ROS/RNS measurement  The hydrogen peroxide assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, S0038) was used to detect H 2 O 2  in the solution, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 100 μl of detection reagent was added to 50 μl of samples and standards, followed by a 30 min incubation at room temperature. The absorbance was measured using a microplate reader (Tecan Infinite E plex) with wavelength settings of 560 nm for excitation. Nitrite concentration quantification was performed using the Griess reagent system (Beyotime Biotechnology, S0021S) according to the manufacturer’s protocol, wherein 50 μl aliquots of both Griess Reagent I and II were mixed with 50 μl test samples and incubated for 10 minutes before measuring absorbance at 540 nm using a Tecan Infinite E plex microplate reader. Hydroxyl radical generation following cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) exposure was assessed through the terephthalic acid (TA) fluorescence assay (Sigma), where 2 mM TA solution (pH = 10.16) was irradiated with CAP and the subsequent formation of fluorescent 2-hydroxyterephthalic acid (HTA) was quantified by fluorescence spectroscopy with 310 nm excitation and emission scanning from 350–550 nm.    Cell Isolation and in vitro assay  Neutrophil isolation was performed using magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) technology with species-specific markers, where mouse neutrophils were positively selected using Ly6G Microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–097-658) while human neutrophils were enriched via CD16 Microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–045-701), both achieving ≥90% purity as confirmed by flow cytometric analysis, with subsequent culture of the isolated cells in complete RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) under standard conditions. Both murine and human neutrophils were resuspended in Hank’s balanced saline solution (HBSS) containing 2% of bovine serum albumin (BSA) and calcium. Cell suspensions contained >95% of viable neutrophils, as established by flow cytometry. For coculture studies, MACS-sorted neutrophils were incubated with bladder cancer cells, with post-treatment fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and crystal violet (0.5%) staining for microscopic imaging analysis, while proliferation assays involved 96-hour incubation with CAP-activated medium followed by sulforhodamine B (SRB) colorimetric assessment performed per standard protocols.  Mouse neutrophils were isolated from female C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old).  Human neutrophils were isolated from tumor specimens or peripheral blood of consented patients.  For pharmacological inhibitor experiments, mouse neutrophils were pre-incubated for 1 hour prior to CAP treatment with the following inhibitors: Nrf2 inhibitor ML385 (5 μM, Selleckchem, S8790), HIF-1α inhibitor KC7F2 (20 μM, Selleckchem, S7946) or NF-κB inhibitor BAY11–7082 (5 μM, Selleckchem, S7352). Following inhibitor pre-incubation, cells were treated with CAP-activated medium. Control groups received an equivalent volume of vehicle (DMSO, final concentration < 0.1%).    Confocal microscopy  For immunofluorescence staining of human TANs, neutrophils were sorted from dissociated human bladder cancer tissues by MACS, incubated onto poly-L-lysine-coated glass slides, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin, and incubated with anti-human CD66b antibody (Abcam, ab300122) overnight at 4°C, followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Beyotime Biotechnology, C1006). For mouse TANs, Ly6G +  cells were sorted from dissociated mouse bladder tumors, processed identically, and stained with anti-mouse Ly6G antibody (Abcam, ab238132) followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody. All slides were mounted and images were acquired using a confocal microscope (Andor Dragonfly 200) and analyzed with ImageJ software.  For mitophagy and mitochondrial function assays, neutrophils or sorted TANs were seeded onto poly-L-lysine-coated coverslips and treated differently. Mitophagy was detected using the Mitophagy Detection Kit (DOJINDO, MD01), and mitochondrial membrane potential was assessed using the JC-1 assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, C2003S), following the manufacturers’ protocols. After staining, coverslips were washed, mounted with DAPI-containing mounting medium, and imaged by confocal microscopy. Image analysis was performed using ImageJ.    Histology and immunofluorescence analysis  Standard histological evaluation was performed through hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of 4% paraformaldehyde-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor sections which were subsequently imaged using a VS120 Olympus microscope equipped with OlyVIA software. While immunofluorescence analysis involved processing of 10-μm cryosections through room temperature dehydration and PBS rehydration followed by 1-hour blocking, overnight incubation with primary antibodies at 4°C, 1-hour room temperature incubation with AlexaFluor-conjugated secondary antibodies, DAPI nuclear counterstaining, and final visualization and quantification using an Andor Dragonfly 200 confocal imaging system.    Western blot  Cells were collected and lysed with RIPA buffer supplemented with PMSF (Beyotime Biotechnology). The protein concentration was determined with BCA Protein Assay Reagent Kit. Total protein of each sample was separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. Sequentially, the membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) defatted milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.05% Tween (TBS-T) for 1 h at room temperature followed by incubation with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C with shaking. Membranes were rinsed in TBS-T and secondary horseradish peroxidase-conjugated antibodies were applied for 1 h at room temperature with shaking. Membranes were rinsed with TBS-T, and bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence reagent (Bio-Rad) and a chemiluminescence apparatus. The following primary antibodies were used for immunoblotting and immunofluorescence analyses: LC3A/B (D3U4C) XP rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 12741, RRID: AB_2617131), SQSTM1/p62 (D5E2) rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 8025, RRID: AB_10859911), Parkin (Prk8) mouse monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 4211, RRID: AB_2159920), PINK1 (D8G3) rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 6946, RRID: AB_11179069), Atg5 (D5F5U) rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 12994, RRID: AB_2630393), β-Actin (13E5) rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 4970, RRID: AB_2223172), Myeloperoxidase (MPO; E1E7I) XP rabbit monoclonal antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat# 14569, RRID: AB_2798516).    Intracellular ROS detection  Intracellular ROS were measured with the fluorescent probe DCFH-DA (Beyotime Biotechnology, S0033S). After CAP treatment, neutrophils were incubated with fluorescent probes (10 μM) for 30 min in the cell incubator. Finally, the cells were analyzed with a flow cytometry and the data analysis was performed with Flowjo analysis software.    Mouse XL cytokine array  Neutrophil culture supernatant was obtained as described above, and 111 soluble proteins were quantified using a Mouse XL Cytokine Array Kit (R&D Systems). Protein detection was visualized using a Chemi Reagent Mix (R&D Systems) and a chemiluminescence apparatus. Pixel density was quantified by densiometric analysis using the Image J Software.    Flow cytometry  For the analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, briefly, tumors were dissected from mice, weighed, and digested into single-cell suspension using Type IV Collagenase and DNase. For the neutrophil panel, cells were incubated with CD11b and Ly6G antibodies in the dark for 30 minutes at 4°C and quantified using flow cytometry. For the T cell panel, cells were incubated with CD3 and CD8 antibodies. Only for the T cell function panel, the cells were resuspended in permeabilization solution and stained intracellularly with Granzyme B antibodies in the dark for 1 hour at 4°C. Flow cytometry analysis was performed with a BeckmanCoulter CytoFLEX, and the results were analyzed using CytExpert and FlowJo software. After activating with CAP at 37°C and 5% CO 2 , neutrophils were washed in PBS and incubated with Mitophagy Dye (DOJINDO, MD01) or JC-1 dye (Beyotime Biotechnology, C2003S) for 30 min individually. Samples were washed twice in PBS and immediately analyzed by flow cytometry. The fluorescence of samples was measured in a flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software. For flow cytometry, the following fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies were used: APC anti-human CD45 antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 304012, RRID: AB_314400), FITC anti-human CD66b antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 305104, RRID: AB_314496), FITC anti-mouse CD3 antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 100203, RRID: AB_312660), APC anti-mouse CD8a antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 100712, RRID: AB_312751), PerCP/Cy5.5 anti-human/mouse Granzyme B recombinant antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 372212, RRID: AB_2728379), APC anti-mouse/human CD11b antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 101212, RRID: AB_312795), PE anti-mouse Ly-6G antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 127607, RRID: AB_1186104).    Three-dimensional spheroid culture  Three-dimensional spheroid formation was achieved using an optimized hanging drop technique, wherein 15–30 μl aliquots of single-cell suspension containing 0.24% methylcellulose were carefully pipetted onto culture dish lids and inverted over PBS-filled base dishes to maintain humidity, followed by incubation under standard culture conditions (37°C, 5% CO 2 ) for 5 days with daily monitoring until aggregate formation; mature spheroids were then gently transferred to 96-well plates for confocal microscopic imaging at 10× magnification. While for neutrophil-bladder cancer cell coculture experiments, neutrophils were prelabeled with CFDA-SE [5(6)-carboxyfluorescein diacetate succinimidyl ester] fluorescent dye prior to spheroid formation to enable subsequent tracking and visualization.    ELISA  ELISA kits were used to assay the levels of mouse IL-12 (Cat: M3062; Elabscience), mouse TNF-α (Cat: M3063; Elabscience), and mouse IL-6 (Cat: M0044; Elabscience) in tumor tissue according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, the standard solution and samples were added to the plate and incubated for 2 hours at room temperature. Then, the wells were aspirated and washed 5 times with wash buffer, and the conjugate was added to each well followed by incubation for 2 hours. After five washes, the substrate solution and stop solution were added successively with a thorough mixture. The optical density of each well was determined using a microplate reader.    Analysis of OCR with the seahorse XF platform  To evaluate the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), neutrophils in Seahorse XF RPMI Medium without glucose (Agilent Technologies) were seeded in a 96-well XF Cell Culture Microplate (Agilent Technologies) pre-coated with poly-L-lysine. Cells were left to adhere for one hour at 37°C without CO 2 . Neutrophils were activated with CAP, and OCR were then measured on a Seahorse XF Analyser (Agilent Technologies) in basal conditions, and upon the sequential addition of oligomycin (1.5 μM), Carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy)-phenylhydrazone (FCCP, 3 μM), and rotenone/antimycin A (1 μM).    Transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq)  Mouse neutrophils were purified from tumors upon MACS cell sorting, and then neutrophils were treated with CAP and cocultured for 12 hours. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher, 15596018) following the manufacturer’s procedure. The total RNA quantity and purity were analyzed with a Bioanalyzer 2100 and RNA 6000 Nano LabChip Kit (Agilent, CA, USA, 5067–1511), and high-quality RNA samples with RIN > 7.0 were used to construct a sequencing library. After mRNA purification and cDNA amplification, we performed the 2× 150 bp paired-end sequencing (PE150) on an Illumina Novaseq 6000 (LC-Bio Technology CO., Ltd., Hangzhou, China) following the vendor’s recommended protocol. Gene differential expression analysis was performed by DESeq2 software between two different groups (and by edgeR between two samples). Genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05 and absolute fold change ≥2 were considered differentially expressed genes.    Single-cell RNA-seq and data processing  Tumors from MB49-bearing mice with different treatment were digested in tissue dissociation solution according to the manufacturer’s instructions and single-cell suspensions were obtained. Tumor-infiltrating CD45 +  cells were enriched by FACS. Cell suspensions were counted with Countess 3 automated cell counter to determine cell concentration and viability. Cells were then loaded onto a microfluidic chip and scRNA-seq libraries were constructed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The scRNA-seq libraries were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq X10 instrument with 150 bp paired end reads. Raw sequencing reads were processed to generate gene expression profiles using CeleScope v1.5.2 (Singleron Biotechnologies) with default parameters. Adapters and polyA tails were trimmed before aligning reads to the mouse GRCm38. Reads with the same cell barcode, UMI, and gene were grouped together to generate the UMI count matrix.  Single-cell RNA-seq datasets ( GSE267718  and  GSE201425 ) were downloaded from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Only samples from patients with matched peripheral blood and tumor tissue scRNA-seq profiles were retained for subsequent analyses. Raw UMI count matrices were imported into R(v4.5.0) and analyzed using Seurat (v5.2.1). For each sample, seurat objects were created from raw UMI count matrices. Doublets were identified using the scDblFinder package (v1.24.0) and excluded from downstream analyses. Quality control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells, retaining cells with nFeature_RNA > 500 and < 6000 and mitochondrial transcript fraction (percent.mt) < 25%. Then, data were normalized using SCTransform with default parameters. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed, and the top 30 PCs (dims = 1:30) were used for downstream analyses. To mitigate batch effects across samples, batch correction was carried out using the Harmony algorithm on the PCA embeddings.  After Harmony batch correction on the PCA space (dims = 1:30), we constructed the k-nearest neighbor graph using FindNeighbors (dims = 1:30) and performed graph-based clustering using FindClusters (resolution = 1.6 for  GSE267718  and 1.0 for  GSE201425 ). UMAP embeddings were generated using RunUMAP (dims = 1:30) for visualization. Differential gene expression analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the SCTransform-normalized expression values. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and genes were considered differentially expressed if they met all of the following criteria: adjusted P value (padj) < 0.05, log2 fold change (log2FC) ≥ 1, and pct > 0.25. Cell types were annotated based on canonical marker gene expression. Heatmaps were visualized using ComplexHeatmap (v2.26.0).    Statistical analysis  Data analyses in the study were performed using GraphPad Prism. Figure legends specified the means and standard deviations, data presentation and statistical strategies, as well as all experimental repetitions and numbers of specimens. Two-tailed Student’s t-tests were used for two-group comparisons; one-way or two-way ANOVA for multiple groups; log-rank test for survival analyses; Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-parametric data; RNA-seq analyses were performed using DESeq2 with FDR correction.  P  < 0.05 was considered as statistically significant (* P  < 0.05; ** P  < 0.01; *** P  < 0.001; **** P  < 0.0001). Dying cells initiate DLL4–Notch signaling to drive tumor repopulation after insufficient thermal ablation of papillary thyroid carcinoma Background  Although lacking high-quality clinical evidence, the use of thermal ablation for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is increasing. Emerging evidence suggests that thermal ablation may accelerate tumor progression in some patients, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. This study aims to explore the mechanisms of tumor repopulation following thermal ablation and identify possible intervention strategies.    Materials and methods  In vitro and in vivo models were employed to simulate tumor repopulation after thermal ablation and investigate mechanisms. Clinicopathological features of post-ablation surgical specimens were analyzed, and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics was conducted. Time-lapse imaging and RNA-seq explored how dying cells influence surviving cells. qPCR, WB, IHC, and flow cytometry validated molecular mechanisms, while enChIP-MS identified upstream regulators.    Results  Post-ablation PTC tissue showed significantly higher proliferative potential. Heat-induced dying cells promote surviving cell repopulation in a contact-dependent manner. Dying cells upregulated DLL4, activating Notch signaling in surviving cells and driving proliferation. Clinical specimens and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics revealed elevated Notch activity in tumor cells adjacent to the ablation bed. Inhibition of DLL4–Notch signaling attenuated the dying cell–induced proliferative advantage in vitro and in vivo. enChIP–MS showed HNRNPU enrichment at the DLL4 promoter after heat treatment. Mechanistically, heat treatment increased HNRNPU nuclear enrichment and binding at the DLL4 promoter, facilitating DLL4 transcription.    Conclusion  Heat-induced dying cells promote tumor repopulation after insufficient thermal ablation in PTC through the DLL4–Notch pathway. With the expanding use of thermal ablation, understanding and mitigating its limitations is essential for clinical advancement.    Supplementary Information  The online version contains supplementary material available at  https://doi.org/10.1186/s12964-026-03106-5 .     Keywords:  Papillary thyroid carcinoma, Thermal ablation, Notch, DLL4, Dying cells      status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Received 2026 Apr 26; Accepted 2026 Jul 19; Collection date 2026.       Introduction  The incidence of thyroid cancer is rising rapidly, making it one of the most common cancers worldwide, and it has reached the third highest incidence among all malignant cancers in China [ 1 ]. Despite the high incidence, papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) generally has a favorable prognosis, with over 90% of patients achieving a survival time exceeding 10 years [ 2 ]. As a result, there is growing interest in evaluating more conservative treatment strategies, such as active surveillance [ 3 ] and thermal ablation [ 4 ].  Thermal ablation has been widely adopted for the treatment of benign thyroid nodules and for palliative management of locally recurrent or metastatic PTC [ 5 ,  6 ]. Although preliminary data indicate promising effects of thermal ablation for PTC [ 7 ,  8 ], there are significant concerns regarding its efficacy, safety, and long-term outcomes as we proposed [ 9 ]. An increasing amount of evidence based on post-ablation pathological samples revealed a substantial proportion of patients possess residual viable cancer cells, increased rates of lymph node metastasis, and, even accelerated tumor progression in certain patients [ 10 – 12 ]. Moreover, larger tumor size and multifocal nodules are associated with a significantly increased risk of recurrence after ablation [ 13 ,  14 ]. However, the reasons underlying this accelerated progression remain unclear.  Mechanistically, thermal ablation induces cell death through the release of heat, with temperatures exceeding 45 °C leading to various forms of cellular damage [ 15 ]. However, due to temperature gradients and the heat sink effect [ 16 ], some regions may experience sublethal temperatures, resulting in incomplete ablation and residual tumor cells. Additionally, the thyroid’s small size and proximity to critical structures make complete ablation challenging [ 17 ], which increases the likelihood of a proportion of cells undergoing programmed cell death and leaving residual tumor cells. During the dying process, cells underlying programmed cell death may send out signals to instruct tissue regeneration and homeosis. However, the process can be hijacked by cancer cells. Previous studies have indicated that dying tumor cells generated by various cancer treatments can secrete signals that significantly influence therapy efficacy and even potentiate tumor repopulation [ 18 – 20 ]. Thermal ablation inevitably generates large numbers of dying cells, yet their potential influence on therapy efficacy has not been thoroughly investigated.  In this study, we demonstrated that dying PTC cells generated by thermal ablation promote tumor repopulation by activating the Notch signaling pathway. We further identified the unique role of thermal ablation-induced dying tumor cells in enhancing tumor repopulation through direct cell-cell interactions, rather than releasing soluble factors as seen in dying cells generated by cytotoxic therapies. Specifically, dying cells upregulated DLL4, which subsequently activated the Notch pathway in surviving cells, promoting their proliferation. Furthermore, we observed that dying cells increased nuclear enrichment of HNRNPU and its recruitment to the DLL4 promoter, thereby boosting DLL4 transcription and amplifying its expression. In summary, our study reveals the biological mechanisms underlying tumor repopulation following insufficient thermal ablation of PTC and identifies potential therapeutic targets to support future intervention strategies.    Materials and methods   Patients and tissue specimens  We retrospectively collected clinicopathological data and tissue samples of PTC patients who had received thermal ablation treatment prior to surgery and patients who received upfront surgery at a 1:9 ratio from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center. This study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (NO. B2024-552-01). All procedures performed during the study adhere to the principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki as revised in 2013.    Heat treatment, co-culture system establishment, and reporter cell assays  To simulate thermal ablation in vitro, we employed the approach similar to those previously used in studies of liver cancer ablation [ 21 ,  22 ]. In brief, PTC cells were seeded in 6-well or 24-well plates and cultured for 18 h. The medium was removed and replaced with preheated medium at 55 °C, and plates were transferred to an incubator set at 55 °C for 5 min to mimic the thermal ablation process. To minimize confounding factors from cytokines in FBS, the medium was replaced with low-serum medium (3% FBS) after heat treatment for further culture. Details on the temperature optimization process are shown in Supplementary Figure S1A.  To mimic the in vivo scenario where the majority of PTC cells undergo cell death post-ablation, we drew upon previously established co-culture systems used in studies of dying cells and applied a similar approach [ 19 ,  23 ]. In brief, a small number of reporter cells (1,000 cells/well) were co-cultured with heat-treated dying cells (feeder cells, 50,000 cells/well) immediately after heat treatment with low-serum DMEM (for TPC-1) or RPMI 1640 (for KTC-1 or Nthy-ori-3-1) medium (3% FBS). After three days post-co-culture, 200 µL of 0.15 mg/mL D-luciferin solution was added to each well, and bioluminescence imaging was conducted using the IVIS Spectrum system for quantitative analysis. Where indicated, pharmacologic inhibitors or antibody were added immediately after heat treatment, at the time of reporter-cell seeding, and maintained throughout the co-culture period until the readout. For inhibitor/antibody experiments, reporter-cell proliferation was evaluated relative to the corresponding reporter-cell-alone group under matched treated or untreated conditions. Two PTC reporter cell lines (Luc-TPC-1 and Luc-KTC-1) were established by lentiviral transduction of the eGFP-luciferase construct followed by puromycin selection, as described in the Supplementary Materials and Methods. Validation data for tumor cell bioluminescence quantification can be found in Supplementary Figure S1B.    Time-lapse imaging  FUCCI (Fluorescent Ubiquitination-based Cell Cycle Indicator) reporter cells were generated by lentiviral transduction of the FastFUCCI construct followed by puromycin selection, as described in the Supplementary Materials and Methods. FUCCI reporter cells were co-cultured with heat-treated dying cells and placed in a 37 °C humidified chamber with 5% CO₂. Dynamic cell interactions were recorded using an HIS-SIM microscope, with images captured every 20 min. The FUCCI system labels cells at different stages of the cell cycle [ 24 ], allowing observation of dynamic changes in the cell cycle of the FUCCI labeled cells.    Animal experiments  All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center. Male BALB/c nude mice (6–8 weeks old) were subcutaneously inoculated in the right flank with human TPC-1 cells (1 × 10^7). Tumor volume was calculated as V = (length × width^2)/2. When tumors reached ~ 100 mm^3, microwave ablation (MWA) was performed under tribromoethanol anesthesia (i.p.) using a 17G MWA needle (Changcheng Microwave System Engineering Co., Ltd.) at 75 W for 15 s. The ablation probe was maintained at the tumor center throughout the procedure.  To minimize bias from tumor size–dependent ablation variability, mice were volume-matched into eight pairs immediately after MWA and assigned to receive enoticumab (human anti-DLL4 monoclonal antibody; 2.5 mg/kg, i.p.) or isotype IgG at the same dose, starting immediately after MWA and repeated every 4 days. Tumor volumes were measured at each dosing time point. Mice were euthanized on day 20 post MWA; tumors were excised, weighed, and processed for downstream analyses. Additional mice were euthanized at 72 h post MWA for histological analyses.    Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), engineered DNA-binding molecule-mediated chromatin immunoprecipitation (enChIP) and enChIP-MS  Cells were harvested 18 h post-heat treatment and fixed with formaldehyde (#12606S, CST). ChIP assays were performed using the ChIP Kit (#56383S, CST) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Immunoprecipitation was carried out using anti-HNRNPU antibodies to pull down the HNRNPU-DNA complexes. Following de-crosslinking and DNA purification, PCR was used to evaluate HNRNPU binding to target sequences. Primer sequences for PCR are listed in Supplementary Table S1.  enChIP effectively identifies specific genomic regions using CRISPR/dCas9 technology, enabling detailed analysis of chromatin complexes associated with these regions [ 25 ]. For enChIP, the dCas9-3xFLAG stable cell line with sgRNA targeting the DLL4 promoter was subjected to ChIP as described above. Immunoprecipitation was performed using anti-3xFLAG antibodies to pull down complexes containing dCas9-3xFLAG and the DLL4 promoter region.  In enChIP-MS, immunoprecipitated complexes obtained with anti-3xFLAG antibodies were boiled in 1x SDS buffer and subjected to SDS-PAGE. The entire gel lane was excised, and pre-processed samples were analyzed by nano-liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Data were acquired through data-dependent analysis and processed using PLGS software (Waters). The Mascot search engine was used to search the peak lists against the NCBI database. To ensure accuracy, common keratin contaminants were excluded, and the top 10% of enriched proteins, ranked by p-value, were selected for further analysis.    Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics and spatial ROI–distance analysis of NOTCH pathway module scores  A tumor specimen from Patient 6 was profiled using the 10x Genomics Xenium 5 K in situ spatial transcriptomics platform. Xenium generates single-cell spatial expression matrices by integrating in situ optical barcode decoding with high-resolution image segmentation. In addition to the standard 5 K panel, 50 custom genes were included to enhance cell-state characterization; the full gene list is provided in Table S2. The Xenium cell-by-gene count matrix and spatial coordinates (centroids) were analyzed using Seurat (v5). Data were normalized (NormalizeData), 2,000 highly variable genes were selected (FindVariableFeatures), and scaled with regression of available technical covariates (nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, cell_area, control_probe_counts, unassigned_codeword_counts). Dimensionality reduction was performed by PCA (50 PCs), followed by graph-based clustering (dims 1:20; resolution = 0.15) and UMAP visualization (dims 1–20). Cluster marker genes were identified using FindAllMarkers and annotated based on canonical markers and pathway enrichment patterns.  Genes belonging to the NOTCH signaling pathway gene set (REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_NOTCH, MSigDB) were curated, and only genes present in the Xenium expression matrix were retained. Per-cell NOTCH module scores were computed using AddModuleScore (R Seurat package) and subsequently standardized across cells by z-score transformation.  For ROI–distance analysis, the ablation/necrotic region was first determined on matched H&E sections by a board-certified pathologist. Guided by this annotation, the ROI boundary was manually delineated interactively in R as a polygon on the Xenium spatial map and saved for reproducibility. For each cell, the Euclidean distance to the ROI polygon was computed as the minimum distance from the cell centroid to the polygon boundary; cells located inside the ROI were assigned a distance of 0. Distances were binned in 50 μm increments (bin center = (bin + 0.5) × 50 μm), and bins containing fewer than 50 cells were excluded. For each distance bin, the median z-scored NOTCH module score was computed and visualized as a distance–response curve with LOESS smoothing (span = 0.80). Monotonic associations between distance and module score were assessed using Spearman correlation. To visualize spatial gradients while preserving per-cell trends, coordinates were aggregated into 40 μm × 40 μm square tiles. Within each tile, the median per-cell z-scored NOTCH module score was computed (tiles with fewer than 5 cells were excluded). Color scales were clipped to the 5th–95th percentiles, with out-of-range values squished to the limits, and the ROI boundary was overlaid on the heatmap.    RNA sequencing, bioinformatics analysis and statistics  RNA sequencing was performed on heat-treated dying tumor cells and reporter cells isolated by FACS from the co-culture system. Three replicates were included in each group. Sequencing libraries were prepared using the Illumina ®  Stranded mRNA Prep Ligation according to the manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform with paired-end 150-bp reads (PE150). Raw paired-end reads were trimmed and quality controlled using fastp before downstream analysis.  Bioinformatics analysis was performed using R version 4.5.2. Thyroid cancer patients’ data from the TCGA cohort ( n  = 512) were obtained from the  GEPIA  database ( http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/ ). Data are presented as mean ± standard error of mean (SEM) from at least three independent experiments unless otherwise specified. Unpaired and paired t-tests were used for statistical comparisons as appropriate. The Pearson correlation coefficient (r value) was calculated to assess the linear relationship between variables. Log-Rank test was used for survival analysis. GraphPad Prism 9 software was used for data analysis and graphical representation. Results   Heat-induced dying cells enhance tumor repopulation  Previous studies have shown that a substantial proportion of PTC patients still exhibit residual tumor foci during subsequent thyroid cancer surgery after thermal ablation, and some patients’ residual lesions display increased proliferative and invasive capabilities [ 10 ,  12 ]. In our center, we identified 10 PTC patients who underwent thermal ablation prior to surgery. Interestingly, these patients exhibited similar phenomena in their postoperative pathology, including a higher rate of tumor residuals at the ablation sites (7/10), unusual capsule invasion (8/10), and lymph node metastasis (9/10) (Table  1 ). Notably, the tumors of these patients displayed a strong proliferative potential, with an average Ki-67 positive cell percentage of 7.86%. To further investigate this, we randomly matched each patient’s tissue sample with 9 samples from PTC patients who underwent upfront surgery during the same period and compared their Ki-67 expression (The clinicopathological characteristics of the ablation and surgery-only control cohorts are summarized in Supplementary Table S5). The results showed that the Ki-67 expression in thermal ablation-treated patients was significantly higher than that in the control cohort (Fig.  1 A, approximately 1%, which is consistent with previously reported Ki-67 levels in PTC patients [ 26 ]). Additionally, representative mIHC image of a patient receiving thermal ablation demonstrated a marked increase in the proliferation marker Ki-67 in PTC cells (marked by TTF1) adjacent to the ablation site (Fig.  1 B), further suggesting a potential proliferation-promoting role of the thermal ablation site. To determine whether this effect was initiated by the heat-induced dying tumor cells, we established an in vitro co-culture system by co-culturing heat-treated dying cells and reporter cells (expressing GFP and luciferase for identification and quantification, Figure S1). Reporter cells co-cultured with dying cells exhibited significantly increased proliferation after three days (Luc-TPC-1 and Luc-KTC-1, Fig.  1 C-D). Interestingly, heat-induced dying benign thyroid epithelial cells (Nthy-Ori-3-1) also significantly promoted the proliferation of PTC reporter cells (Luc-TPC-1 and Luc-KTC-1, Fig.  1 E-F), indicating that this phenomenon may apply to both benign and malignant thyroid cells. To investigate changes in reporter cells after co-culture with dying cells, reporter cells from the co-culture system were enriched by flow cytometry and subjected to bulk RNA sequencing, followed by GO enrichment analysis. The enriched signaling pathways were largely associated with conditions required for cell proliferation, such as DNA replication, strand elongation, cell cycle progression, and mismatch repair (Fig.  1 G), suggesting that these cells acquired an active proliferative potential. This was further confirmed by EdU assays, which demonstrated that more reporter cells co-cultured with dying cells entered a rapid proliferation state (Fig.  1 H-I). To further determine whether this dying cell–mediated effect could attribute to a specific mode of cell death, we pharmacologically inhibited major cell-death pathways in the co-culture system. Specifically, inhibitors of autophagy (3-MA), apoptosis (Z-VAD-FMK), necroptosis (Nec-1), and ferroptosis (Fer-1) were added to the co-culture system immediately after heat treatment, at the time of reporter-cell seeding, and were maintained throughout the co-culture period. Under both inhibitor-treated and untreated settings, reporter-cell proliferation in the co-culture group was evaluated relative to the corresponding reporter-cell-alone group. Notably, inhibition of any single pathway did not attenuate the proliferation-promoting effect induced by dying cells in either TPC-1 reporter cells (Fig.  1 J–M) or KTC reporter cells (Fig.  1 N–Q). Collectively, these data indicate that heat-induced dying cells robustly enhance tumor repopulation. Interestingly, culturing reporter cells with conditioned media derived from dying cells did not effectively promote their growth (Figs.  2 B-C), indicating that the transmission of the proliferative signal from dying cells is contact-dependent. To further explore this, we labeled cells with the FUCCI system, which indicates cell cycle phases in real-time when monitored with time-lapse imaging (Fig.  2 D). Time-lapse imaging revealed that FUCCI cells rapidly entered the proliferation phase upon contact with dying cells (Fig.  2 E, Video S1). Cell cycle analysis showed a significant shortening of the G1 phase in FUCCI cells after contact with dying cells (Fig.  2 F), suggesting accelerated cell proliferation. The results revealed significant enrichment of several signaling pathways related to stemness and stress response in the dying cells, including the Notch-related signaling pathway (Signaling by NOTCH, Fig.  3 A). Consistently, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) further demonstrated a significant activation of this pathway in dying cells (Fig.  3 B; NES = 1.77,  p  = 0.001, q = 0.009). The Notch signaling pathway is a crucial regulator of cell fate and tumorigenesis and transmits signals through a contact-dependent manner [ 27 ,  28 ], which is consistent with our observation of contact-dependent interactions between dying cells and surviving cells (Fig.  2 ). We subsequently examined the expression of four NICDs, which mediate Notch pathway activation, in reporter cells. All four NICDs were significantly upregulated in reporter cells co-cultured with dying tumor cells compared with those co-cultured with untreated tumor cells (Fig.  3 C), confirming the activation of the Notch pathway. Further analysis showed that HES1, a marker of Notch pathway activation, was markedly upregulated in the surviving cells (Fig.  3 D-G), suggesting a key role for the Notch signaling pathway in this process. When the Notch inhibitor DAPT was added to the co-culture system, the dying cell–induced proliferative advantage was significantly reduced (Fig.  3 H–I), indicating that the Notch signaling pathway plays a critical role in the rapid proliferation of surviving cells induced by dying tumor cells. Interestingly, dying benign thyroid epithelial cells also activated HES1 expression in reporter cells (Figure S2A-B), and DAPT effectively inhibited reporter cell proliferation (Figure S2C-D), although this effect was not significant in Luc-TPC-1 cells. Heat-induced dying tumor cells activate the Notch pathway in surviving cells by upregulating DLL4  To investigate how dying cells activate Notch signaling in reporter cells, we examined the expression of canonical Notch ligands in dying cells after heat treatment. DLL4 was robustly upregulated in heat-induced dying tumor cells as well as dying benign thyroid epithelial cells (Fig.  4 A–C). Consistent with a potential pro-tumorigenic role of DLL4 in thyroid cancer, analysis of the TCGA thyroid cancer cohort showed that higher DLL4 expression was associated with poorer overall survival (Fig.  4 D). Flow cytometry further confirmed a marked increase in DLL4 protein expression after heat treatment (Fig.  4 E-F). To test whether DLL4 induction is functionally required for the proliferative effect, we used a CRISPRi system to generate stable DLL4 knockdown cells. As shown in Fig.  4 E–F, heat treatment increased DLL4 protein levels, and in this same heat-treatment setting, heat-treated sgiNC cells were used as the control (Fig.  4 G–H). Compared with the heat-treated sgiNC group, heat-treated sgiDLL4 cells showed markedly reduced DLL4 fluorescence intensity by flow cytometry, confirming effective DLL4 knockdown at the protein level. Importantly, dying feeder cells carrying a non-targeting sgRNA (sgiNC) retained their ability to enhance reporter-cell proliferation during co-culture, whereas DLL4 knockdown in dying cells significantly blunted this proliferation-promoting effect (Fig.  4 I-J), indicating that DLL4 is a key mediator of dying cell–induced tumor repopulation signals. Furthermore, to determine whether DLL4 upregulation and Notch activation are also observed in clinical specimens, we performed mIHC on ablation-treated PTC patients with residual PTC cells at the ablation region ( n  = 7; Table 1) to assess DLL4 and the Notch activation marker HES1. DLL4 and HES1 signals in PTC cells were detectable adjacent to the ablation bed in 4/7 patients, and representative staining patterns from two patients are shown in Fig.  4 K. Heat-induced dying tumor cells upregulate DLL4 expression by enriching HNRNPU binding to the DLL4 promoter  To determine whether DLL4 upregulation was dependent on activated transcription or suppressed RNA decay, we first treated cells with actinomycin D to inhibit RNA transcription. The upregulation of DLL4 following heat treatment was significantly suppressed after supplementation with actinomycin D (Fig.  6 A-B), indicating that DLL4 expression is highly dependent on transcriptional activation. Since the transcriptional regulation of DLL4 has not been systematically studied, we employed the CRISPR/Cas9 system-based enChIP method [ 25 ] to identify proteins that specifically bind to the DLL4 promoter region after thermal ablation, aiming to find factors that regulate DLL4 transcription (Fig.  6 C). We constructed four sgRNAs that target the DLL4 promoter region to identify potential transcriptional regulatory targets (Fig.  6 D-E, Figure S4). enChIP-PCR confirmed successful pull-down of the DLL4 promoter region (Fig.  6 F). enChIP-MS identified 805 proteins (Table S6) that bind to the promoter region of DLL4. Further signaling enrichment analysis revealed that the majority of the pathways were related to mRNA transcriptional regulation (Fig.  6 G, Table S7), supporting the specificity of the promoter-centered capture. Discussion  In this study, we provide novel insights into the biological mechanisms driving tumor repopulation and relapse following insufficient thermal ablation of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). We demonstrate that dying tumor cells promote the proliferation of neighboring surviving cells in a contact-dependent manner, which is mediated by the activation of the DLL4-Notch signaling pathway. Moreover, increased nuclear enrichment and promoter binding of HNRNPU play a critical role in DLL4 upregulation (Fig.  7 ). In summary, our study underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of the biological consequences of thermal ablation and careful consideration when selecting treatment strategies for PTC.    Fig. 7   The proposed model of this study                   As a minimally invasive method that induces tumor cell death through heat damage, thermal ablation has been widely applied to treat various solid tumor types for the last 30 years, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), renal cancer, lung cancer, and other cancer types [ 29 ]. However, even in HCC, where thermal ablation has been widely used and demonstrated promising outcomes, insufficient ablation remains a major challenge [ 30 ]. Numerous studies have shown that insufficient ablation may accelerate the progression of residual tumor cells and significantly reduce overall survival [ 31 ,  32 ]. With the increasing use of thermal ablation in recent years, this challenge no longer seems limited to liver cancer, as similar issues have also been observed in PTC. Unlike HCC, which is highly malignant, PTC is relatively indolent, and accelerated progression may result in a higher harm-to-benefit ratio for patients. Our results revealed that not only malignant tumor cells but also benign thyroid epithelial cells could promote the proliferation of residual tumor cells (Fig.  1 ). Since thyroid cancer tends to be multifocal, with many small nodules that may not be detected by imaging, this poses an additional risk factor for recurrence following thermal ablation and could partly explain the high recurrence rate of multifocal nodules. Current data indicate that thermal ablation does not offer better outcomes than active surveillance, and its long-term efficacy, as well as the biological consequences, remains uncertain. Together with our findings that heat-induced dying cells could accelerate the progression of residual tumors, caution should be exercised before applying thermal ablation for PTC.  Most anti-tumor therapies achieve their therapeutic goals by inducing cell death. However, numerous studies have shown that cytotoxic therapy-induced dying tumor cells can release biomacromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids that signal surrounding cells, reshaping the tumor microenvironment to promote proliferation, metastasis, and treatment resistance, ultimately leading to treatment failure [ 18 ]. Although the main goal of thermal ablation is to induce rapid coagulative necrosis via high temperature, various limitations can cause some cells to experience sub-lethal temperatures, leading to regulated cell death or even survival. During the dying process of cells undergoing regulated cell death, these dying cells can actively send out signals, but their role and mechanisms in the context of thermal ablation therapy have never been noticed. Our study is the first to demonstrate that dying cells induced by thermal ablation can transmit proliferative signals to surviving cells, ultimately leading to tumor repopulation. Interestingly, this signal is relayed through direct cell-cell contact, which differs from cytotoxic therapy-induced dying cells. Additionally, we observed active migration of surviving tumor cells toward dying cells (Video S1), suggesting that dying cells may release chemotactic factors to attract surviving tumor cells. Notably, we also observed several DNA damage repair-related pathways in the GO analysis of the reporter cell line that co-cultured with dying cells (e.g., Double-strand break repair via break-induced replication pathway, Fig.  1 ). Previous study on dying tumor cells after radiotherapy have suggested that dying cells may initially induce surrounding cells to repair DNA damage, enhancing their survival [ 19 ]. This indicates that this phenomenon may be highly conserved across different dying cells induced by various therapies, though further studies are needed to validate this hypothesis.  Our study reveals a crucial role for DLL4 in the context of tumor repopulation following thermal ablation. DLL4, a canonical ligand of the Notch signaling pathway, is well-documented for its roles in angiogenesis, tumorigenesis, and drug resistance across various cancer types [ 33 ]. Notably, beyond these functions, recent evidence suggests that the sustained expression of DLL4 in tumor cells is closely associated with proliferation. High expression of DLL4 in cervical cancer has been shown to promote sustained tumor cell proliferation and is closely linked to poor prognosis [ 34 ]. Similarly, earlier studies have demonstrated that DLL4 is significantly overexpressed in thyroid cancer, where it plays a critical role in tumorigenesis and angiogenesis [ 35 ]. TCGA data also indicate that high DLL4 expression in thyroid cancer patients is associated with shorter overall survival, and anti-DLL4 (Enoticumab) attenuates post-ablation repopulation in vitro and in vivo (Figs.  4  and  5 ). These findings suggest that targeting DLL4 early after thermal ablation in PTC may be a promising strategy to comprehensively reduce recurrence risk and improve tumor control. Nevertheless, given the essential role of DLL4 in normal vascular and stem cell biology, caution is warranted when considering DLL4 as a therapeutic target. Although preliminary studies have suggested an acceptable safety profile, its long-term safety remains to be established [ 36 ].  Despite these significant findings, there were some limitations to be clarified. The induction and clearance of dying cells in vivo occur rapidly and dynamically, yet obtaining clinical specimens enriched with these cells is particularly challenging. Since it is neither ethical nor clinically feasible to subject patients to immediate surgery or invasive procedures right after thermal ablation solely for research purposes, direct clinical confirmation of our mechanistic insights remains limited. Nevertheless, we elucidate how dying cells induced by thermal ablation of PTC promote the proliferation of surviving cells in this exploratory study, which may help explain why residual tumor foci after thermal ablation warrant careful clinical attention and may inform future intervention strategies. In addition, the patient cohort included in this study was relatively small, and our findings require further validation in larger, independent cohorts. Moreover, because currently available human PTC cell lines cannot establish tumors in immunocompetent mice, and no well-established syngeneic PTC model is currently available to faithfully recapitulate our experimental setting, our in vivo studies were performed using xenograft models in immunodeficient mice. Consequently, the contribution of host immunity to DLL4-mediated tumor repopulation could not be fully evaluated.    Conclusion  In summary, our study demonstrated that heat-induced dying cells promote the repopulation of residual tumor cells through the DLL4-Notch signaling pathway following incomplete thermal ablation of papillary thyroid carcinoma. These results indicate that targeting DLL4 may serve as an effective strategy to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of thermal ablation for PTC. With the increasing use of thermal ablation, understanding and mitigating its limitations are essential for further clinical application.    Supplementary Information

evidence_text:
InSituPy: a framework for histology-guided, multi-sample analysis of single-cell spatial omics data.

Motivation

Spatial omics data provides unprecedented insights into disease biology, yet its complexity introduces significant challenges in data analysis. Comprehensive analysis requires frameworks that integrate diverse modalities and enable joint processing of multiple datasets and corresponding metadata.

Results

To address these challenges, we introduce InSituPy, a versatile and scalable framework for analyzing spatial omics data from the multi-sample level down to the cellular and subcellular level. Its hierarchical data structure organizes all relevant data modalities per sample and links them to their corresponding metadata, enabling scalable analysis of large patient cohorts using spatial omics technologies. Interactive visualization tools within InSituPy enable seamless integration of histopathological expertise, promoting collaborative hypothesis generation in translational research. Additionally, InSituPy includes built-in analytical algorithms and interfaces with external tools, establishing a standardized workflow for multi-sample spatial omics data analysis.

Availability

The Python package InSituPy is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/SpatialPathology/InSituPy) and PyPi (https://pypi.org/project/insitupy-spatial/), and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18459471). Tutorials and documentation for InSituPy are available at https://insitupy.readthedocs.io/. All code to replicate the results shown in this manuscript can be found in the GitHub repository. Scripts to connect QuPath and InSituPy can be found at https://github.com/SpatialPathology/InSituPy-QuPath. All data required to complete the tutorials is publicly available, and functions to download the data have been implemented. A Zulip community chat for user support and discussion is accessible at https://insitupy.zulipchat.com.
