Because the kidney is composed of diverse and highly specialized cell populations, disease mechanisms may manifest through cell type-specific transcriptional alterations. Recent advances in single-cell and snRNA-seq have enabled high-resolution characterization of kidney cell populations and injury-associated transcriptional states. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 These approaches have provided important insights into kidney biology and disease mechanisms, including the identification of rare glomerular cell types such as podocytes that are often underrepresented in conventional transcriptomic studies. 14 However, most single-cell studies of kidney disease have focused on individual disease entities or tissues obtained from nephrectomy specimens, limiting the ability to compare transcriptional alterations across multiple glomerular diseases using diagnostic human biopsy tissues. To address this gap, we performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from patients with 4 major glomerular diseases—MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD—together with control kidney samples. By integrating transcriptomic profiles across disease groups and controls, we aimed to identify both shared and disease-specific transcriptional programs across kidney cell types and to characterize disease-associated cellular states within the human glomerulus. Methods Ethical Considerations and Patient Consent The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Seoul National University Hospital (IRB Nos. H-2203-053-1303 and H-1404-117-575). The study samples were collected from the KORNERSTONE project, a multicenter, prospective cohort study and biobank for glomerular diseases, run under the National Biobank Project of the Republic of Korea. 15 Patients provided informed consent for the collection of the biospecimens, their use in this study, and their use in a public database. The study was conducted under the National Research Project Single Cell Atlas of Immune Disease ( http://www.scaid.org/ ). Kidney Tissue Collection The study subjects were enrolled in the KORNERSTONE project before their first diagnostic kidney biopsy. At our institution, three biopsy cores were typically obtained per patient and first evaluated by an attending nephropathologist for routine clinical diagnostics (light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy). Intact biopsy tissue not required for diagnostic evaluation was immediately snap-frozen at the bedside for biobanking. For snRNA-seq, the remaining cores were used in their entirety; because standard biopsy cores traverse the cortex and may variably extend toward the corticomedullary region, the sequenced material represents mixed cortical regions. We selected patients with preserved kidney function (eGFR ≥ 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ), to minimize disease-nonspecific transcriptomic effects of advanced fibrotic changes. Inclusion required primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without other glomerulonephritis pathologies; patients with urine protein creatinine ratio > 3 g/g (MCD, MN, and DKD) who were immunosuppression-naïve were prioritized to capture active disease. In this study, we included a total of 30 patient kidney samples (from 7 MCD, 6 MN, 13 IgAN, and 4 patients with DKD). Clinical data from the initial visit and treatment initiation were analyzed. For control kidney tissues, we used the normal kidney cortex obtained during radical nephrectomy surgery for kidney cancer. We carefully reviewed the clinical histories to exclude patients with diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease and selected those without proteinuria or obstructive changes in the kidney. To minimize ischemic bias, an intraoperative gun biopsy was obtained from the exposed kidney before renal artery clamping, away from cancerous lesions. Tissues were snap-frozen and delivered to central storage. A total of 7 control patients were included in the study. Results Baseline Characteristics of the Study Subjects We collected data from 37 participants, including individuals with MCD ( n = 7), MN ( n = 6), IgAN ( n = 13), and DKD ( n = 4), as well as a control group ( n = 7). All patient samples were obtained from immunosuppressants-naïve individuals with typical clinical presentations, including primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti- PLA2R antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without another diagnosis. Control kidney tissues were obtained from chemotherapy-naïve patients undergoing nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma, using noncancerous lesions in cortical tissue. The baseline demographics of the study subjects are presented in Supplementary Table S1 . The mean spot urine protein creatinine ratio for each condition was 8.09 ± 4.87 g/g for the MCD group, 7.98 ± 6.49 g/g for the MN group, 1.05 ± 1.36 g/g for the IgAN group, and 3.68 ± 1.78 g/g for the DKD group. The control group had no proteinuria. The baseline eGFR was 89.8 ± 26.8 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 in the study subjects with typical clinical features. We analyzed a total of 333,938 nuclei from biopsy tissues ( Figure 1 a) and identified 12 main cell clusters, annotated based on known canonical markers, including podocytes, PECs, various tubular cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells ( Figure 1 b, c). We next examined the distribution of these subtypes across clinical groups and observed pronounced, disease-specific heterogeneity ( Figure 1 d). To validate these annotations, we compared our data with an external dataset from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project. 9 This comparison revealed a high correlation in marker gene expression profiles ( Supplementary Figure S1 A). Furthermore, upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in our DKD samples showed a similar pattern to those in the Kidney Precision Medicine Project dataset ( Supplementary Figure S1 B). Finally, we performed more detailed subclustering and annotation for each major cell type ( Supplementary Figure S1 C, Supplementary Table S2 ). Figure 1 Study design and single-nucleus transcriptional profiling of kidney biopsy samples from control individuals and patients with glomerular diseases. (a) A schematic showing the overall study design. (b) Human glomerular disease single-nucleus transcriptional atlas ( n = 333,938). UMAP plot showing different cell types identified by snRNA-seq. (c) Dot plot representation of the marker genes for the annotated kidney cell types. The dot size indicates the percentage of relative gene expression for each marker gene. The dot color reflects the average expression level of the specified gene within each cell type. (d) Stacked bar plot showing the per-condition proportions of cell types in each condition. Cell type proportions were calculated relative to the total number of cells within each sample and compared between disease groups and Controls using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Cell types showing statistically significant differences compared with Controls are marked with white asterisks. (e and g) Heatmap illustrating DEGs (|log2FC| > 0.25, adjusted P value < 0.05) categorized into 16 modules through k-means clustering across various cell types in glomerular disease patients in comparison to those in the control group. (e) Heatmap of upregulated DEGs associated with each glomerular disease. Gene modules specific to each glomerular disease are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (g) Heatmap generated by downregulated DEGs, arranged by cell type. Gene modules specific to each cell type are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (f and h) Bar plots of the −log10( P value) from enrichment analysis of DEGs from different modules, as shown in heatmaps. Disease-Dominant, Cell Type-Common, Cell Type-Dominant, and Disease-Common DEGs in Glomerular Diseases Our analysis of DEGs revealed a dichotomous pattern—upregulated DEGs were largely disease-specific but shared across cell types, whereas downregulated DEGs were cell type-specific but common across diseases ( Supplementary Table S3 ). We identified disease-dominant upregulated gene modules enriched in each condition ( Figure 1 e and f; Supplementary Table S4 ). The MCD-dominant module was enriched for transporter-related genes (e.g., SLC13A1 , SLC36A2 ; Module 5). The MN-dominant module included genes associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (e.g., SPP1, VIM ) and the interferon response (e.g., HIF1A, IFNAR2 ; Module 8). The IgAN-dominant module was associated with previously reported pathways, including aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption (Module 2). In DKD, upregulated modules were associated with differentiation and metabolic processes (Module 15) ( Figure 1 f; Supplementary Table S5 ). Representative genes within each module also showed preferential expression in the corresponding disease group at the sample level ( Supplementary Figure S2 A). Module score analysis confirmed significantly higher in scores in the corresponding disease groups compared with others ( Supplementary Figure S2 B). In contrast, downregulated DEGs exhibited a cell type-restricted pattern shared across diseases ( Figure 1 g and 1h; Supplementary Table S4 ). In podocytes, genes related to the actin cytoskeleton (e.g., IQGAP2 , MICAL2 ) 16 , 17 and cell-cell adhesion were reduced (Module 12). In PECs, genes negatively regulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling were downregulated (Module 14). 18 Tubular cells showed decreased expression of metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism, in proximal tubule- and thick ascending limb-specific modules (Modules 1 and 3). 19 , 20 In collecting duct principal cells, the downregulated module included the glucocorticoid receptor and NR4A1 . Endothelial cells demonstrated reduced expression of SPRED2 , with gene ontology analysis indicating negative regulation of the MAPK cascade (Module 9; Supplementary Table S6 ). 21 For each cell type, module scores were significantly lower in diseased samples than in controls, without differences in unrelated cell types ( Supplementary Figure S2 C). Upregulated DEGs were enriched in disease-specific gene modules across glomerular diseases, highlighting the strong disease specificity of transcriptional activation programs ( Figure 3 d). Upregulated DEGs in MN showed enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related genes, whereas IgAN was associated with genes involved in cell-substrate junction assembly ( Figure 3 e). Across diseases, slit diaphragm-associated genes including TJP1 and MAGI2 were consistently downregulated, along with VCL , which contributes to maintenance of the glomerular filtration barrier. 26 , 27 , 28 Additional disease-specific patterns were observed, including detachment-associated genes ( NOX4, TCF21 , and SLIT2 ) 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 in MCD and regeneration-related genes ( PROM1 and PAX8 ) 33 , 34 in DKD ( Figure 3 f and Supplementary Figure S4 A and B and Supplementary Table S9 ). The expression of GADD45A , VIM, and CDH6 , 35 , 36 , 37 which are known to be associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, was found to be specifically elevated in MN. Podocytes were divided into 3 clusters and annotated using marker genes ( Figure 3 g and Supplementary Figure S4 C). One population was characterized by high expression of genes associated with cubilin and amnionless complex, including LRP2 , CUBN , CLCN5 , and PRKCA , and was therefore designated the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure S4 C and D). 38 A similar transcriptional pattern cluster was also observed in podocytes in independent external single-cell datasets, including in patients with chronic kidney disease ( Supplementary Figure S4 E, F, and G). 9 Compared with conventional podocytes, podocyte endocytosis showed increased PAX2 , 39 and reduced expression of CDKN1C , 40 PODXL, and NPHS2, together with higher proliferation module scores ( Supplementary Figure S4 H and I). Importantly, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis cells significantly increased with baseline proteinuria severity (quasibinomial generalized linear model, β = 0.042, P = 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.226), whereas patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment exhibited higher podocyte endocytosis module scores, suggesting an association between this transcriptional state and poor treatment response ( Figure 3 h and i). Accordingly, the gene module score was significantly greater in the MCD and MN groups than in the other glomerular disease groups and the control group ( Figure 3 j). These findings suggest that the activation of endocytosis-related gene programs in podocytes reflects the severity of proteinuria and may also have prognostic implications. We validated the presence of “podocyte endocytosis” at both the transcriptomic and protein levels through the coexpression of LRP2 and NPHS1 in Xenium in situ and megalin (encoded by LRP2 ) and WT1 in immunofluorescence ( Figure 3 k–l and Supplementary Table S7 ). Additionally, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis tended to be higher in glomerular disease in Xenium in situ and IF ( Supplementary Figure S4 J and K). To further characterize the signaling environment associated with podocyte endocytosis, we performed CellChat analysis across glomerular and peri-glomerular populations. Among the inferred pathways, Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling showed preferential communication toward the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure 4 L). Bradykinin signaling originated from multiple glomerular populations, whereas complement and interleukin17 signaling were primarily inferred from juxtaglomerular apparatus cells, PECs, and podocytes. Together, these findings indicate an injury-related signaling microenvironment around podocyte endocytosis cells. Drug2Cell (Wellcome Sanger Institute, Cambridge, UK) 41 identified candidate compounds targeting podocyte endocytosis, including phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors (Apremilast, Roflumilast, and Crisaborole) and the cyclic guanosine monophosphate-modulating agent isosorbide ( Supplementary Figure S4 M), suggesting that modulation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate and cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathways may offer promising therapeutic avenues for targeting podocyte endocytosis-related injury. Trajectory analysis restricted to fibroblast-lineage cells revealed a differentiation continuum from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts present across all disease groups ( Figure 4 d), consistent with the established role of TGF-β signaling in myofibroblast activation. Along this trajectory, gene programs transitioned from mesenchymal differentiation to extracellular matrix organization, reflecting acquisition of myofibroblast functions ( Supplementary Figure S5 B). The expression levels of genes corresponding to the trajectory of the myofibroblast-enriched state and myofibroblast-associated genes, such as SULF1, NOX4, and COL16A1 , were consistently increased in glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 C). Correspondingly, the proportion of myofibroblasts was significantly increased in disease samples compared with controls ( Figure 4 e). A heatmap analysis of fibroblast-associated cell types (e.g., fibroblasts, medullary fibroblasts, adaptive fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts) using their DEGs revealed a gene module (Module 4) that was commonly upregulated across all glomerular diseases (module 4, Supplementary Figure S5 D and Supplementary Table S9 ). This module was significantly enriched for markers of myofibroblasts, TGF-β signaling-related genes, and genes of the Wnt pathway. Consistent with this, functional analysis of the module showed enrichment for biological processes related to myofibroblast function, such as extracellular matrix organization ( Supplementary Figure S5 E). The presence of this shared profibrotic pathway indicates that a common fibrotic program is activated across these diverse glomerular diseases. The myofibroblast gene module score was significantly increased across all glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 F). Importantly, this module score was inversely correlated with eGFR(linear regression r = -0.47, R 2 = 0.22, P -value = 0.003), directly linking the fibrotic signature to declining kidney function ( Figure 4 f). Consistent with this, the proportion of myofibroblasts itself was also higher in the disease groups and was significantly associated with lower baseline (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.013, P -value < 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.339) and follow-up eGFR (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.009, P -value = 0.012, pseudo-R 2 = 0.171) in regression analyses ( Figure 4 g and h). These associations persisted throughout the follow-up period, supporting a potential relationship between myofibroblast expansion and progressive kidney dysfunction. Cell-cell interaction analysis highlighted Periostin pathway as a disease-specific pathway originating from myofibroblasts ( Figure 4 i). This pathway primarily targeted PECs and, in primary glomerular diseases, also affected podocytes ( Figure 4 j). POSTN signaling is implicated in wound healing and fibrosis, 42 , 43 and POSTN-expressing fibroblasts were enriched within diseased glomeruli ( Figure 4 k). Their abundance was significantly associated with both proteinuria severity (R 2 = 0.29, P -value = 0.016) and the proportion of podocyte endocytosis (R 2 = 0.284, P -value = 0.019; Figure 4 l and m). These results indicate that myofibroblasts are common pathogenic cell types in glomerular disease and are associated with a decline in kidney function. Among them, POSTN-expressing myofibroblasts are additionally associated with proteinuria and appear to represent a key cellular component underlying glomerular disease manifestations. To identify potential therapeutic targets for myofibroblasts, we applied the Drug2Cell framework ( Supplementary Figure S5 G). 41 Among the top-ranked candidate compounds, cetirizine and olaratumab were identified as potential modulators of myofibroblast-associated programs. 44 These findings suggest that targeting myofibroblast activity may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for glomerular disease-associated fibrosis. TGF-β and Interferon Signaling in Endothelial Cells are Key to the Pathogenesis of Glomerular Diseases Endothelial cells were subclustered and annotated into 11 distinct cell types using known canonical markers ( Figure 5 a and b). DEGs revealed disease-associated transcriptional modules linked to vascular and immune signaling pathways (Module 2, Figure 5 c and d and Supplementary Table S9 ). Among these, endothelial cells from primary glomerular diseases showed enrichment of vasculogenesis-related programs, whereas disease-specific DEGs were particularly prominent in the MCD and MN groups ( Figure 5 e). Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these signatures were associated with TGF-β signaling and interferon responses, respectively ( Figure 5 f). Gene module scoring showed that TGF-β signaling was most strongly elevated in MN, followed by MCD and DKD ( Figure 5 g), whereas the interferon-α response score was the highest in the MCD group. Both pathways were consistently increased in disease groups compared with controls. When analyzed at the subcluster level, these signaling programs were enriched in glomerular endothelial-related subclusters, with the interferon-α response showing the highest expression in the degenerative endothelial cluster ( Figure 5 h), with interferon-stimulated genes showing particularly high expression in MCD ( Figure 5 i). Discussion This study presents a single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of human biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, comprising 333,938 nuclei obtained from 37 individuals, including 30 treatment-naïve patients with MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD and 7 controls. By profiling diverse kidney cell populations from diagnostic biopsy cores, our dataset provides a comprehensive view of early disease-associated transcriptional changes across glomerular diseases. Another strength of this study is the inclusion of subjects without substantial GFR reduction, which enabled us to compare cell type-specific transcriptomic alterations in relatively early disease states. Our transcriptome data may enhance the understanding of disease-specific pathophysiologic mechanisms of glomerular diseases, which may lead to the discovery of diagnostic or therapeutic biomarkers and common pathological pathways contributing to the progression of chronic kidney disease. This atlas therefore provides a framework for interpreting cell type–specific transcriptional alterations across major glomerular diseases. A notable observation from our analysis was the distinct pattern of transcriptional regulation across diseases and cell types. Upregulated genes tended to form disease-dominant modules, whereas downregulated genes were largely organized by cell type. This pattern suggests that disease-specific signaling programs activate distinct transcriptional responses, whereas functional impairment manifests through loss of cell type-specific gene expression. For example, the MN-dominant transcriptional signature was enriched for epithelial-mesenchymal transition and interferon-γ response pathways, consistent with immune-mediated injury associated with phospholipase A2 receptor autoimmunity 45 , 46 and IgAN modules with MAPK signaling, consistent with MAPK and/or extracellular signal-regulated kinase activation in mesangial injury. 47 Nevertheless, several upregulated modules also exhibited cell type-restricted patterns that complemented the corresponding downregulated programs within the same cell type. For example, proximal tubule modules paired upregulated transport programs with downregulated metabolic programs, suggesting adaptive tubular hypertrophy; endothelial modules paired vasculogenic activation with loss of MAPK negative regulators. We also identified a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and PECs. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells that undergo structural injury and transcriptional remodeling under stress, whereas PECs retain proliferative potential and can respond dynamically to podocyte loss. The hybrid epithelial population was enriched in diseased glomeruli and showed activation of epithelial stress- and proliferation-associated programs, suggesting epithelial plasticity and remodeling within the injured glomerular compartment. This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that pathological activation of PEC signaling pathways can lead to abnormal PEC proliferation and contribute to glomerulosclerosis. Spatial transcriptomic analysis further supported the presence of these cells within diseased glomeruli. Although the lineage relationships of these cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human biopsy data alone, their shared transcriptional features and spatial localization support the existence of an injury-associated hybrid epithelial state in glomerular disease. Our study further identified a podocyte subpopulation characterized by expression of genes involved in protein endocytosis, including the cubilin and amnionless complex components LRP2 and CUBN . 38 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 Previous studies have suggested that podocytes may activate endocytic pathways under protein overload to maintain filtration barrier integrity. Consistent with this, the podocyte endocytosis program was associated with increased proteinuria and remained elevated in patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment. Recent work suggesting that antinephrin autoantibodies in podocytopathies induce nephrin internalization and glomerular endocytic activity provides a potential mechanistic framework, and the prominent MCD enrichment may reflect this adaptive or injury-associated response to slit diaphragm dysfunction. 52 The preferential enrichment of Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling toward this population further suggests an injury-associated microenvironment, consistent with podocyte dedifferentiation features. These findings suggest that this transcriptional state may represent an adaptive but injury-associated podocyte response with potential relevance to disease severity and treatment response. In addition to epithelial injury programs, we observed consistent activation of stromal fibrotic pathways across glomerular diseases. Trajectory analysis suggested differentiation from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts, accompanied by enrichment of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix programs. Notably, the abundance of myofibroblasts correlated with declining kidney function even in patients without severe functional impairment at diagnosis, suggesting that fibrotic remodeling begins early in disease progression. Spatial transcriptomic data further revealed enrichment of POSTN-expressing fibroblasts within diseased glomeruli, supporting the existence of localized fibrotic microenvironments that may promote ongoing glomerular injury. Our data extend previous observations by demonstrating these fibrotic programs at single-cell resolution within human biopsy tissues. Drug2cell analysis further identified candidate compounds targeting disease-associated cellular states, providing a framework for future therapeutic hypothesis generation. The enrichment of distinct pathways in endothelial cells offers potential mechanistic insights into these diseases. For instance, the prominent TGF-β signaling in MN may contribute to the increased glomerular basement membrane thickness characteristic of the disease. 53 Furthermore, the upregulation of major histocompatibility complex molecules in both MCD and MN suggests that endothelial cells may activate antigen-experienced T-cells, implicating T-cell involvement in nephrotic syndrome. 54 , 55 Finally, the elevated interferon signature in MCD could help explain its characteristic steroid sensitivity. 56 There are several limitations in this study. First, glomerular cells comprised a relatively small proportion of total captured nuclei, reflecting the technical challenges of profiling human diagnostic biopsy tissue. Nevertheless, the absolute number of glomerular nuclei ( n = 13,475) was sufficient to identify multiple disease-associated cell states such as podocyte endocytosis. Second, the cohort is heterogeneous with limited samples per disease; however, the use of treatment-naïve diagnostic biopsies allowed us to capture early disease-associated transcriptional programs rarely accessible in human studies and was designed for shared rather than disease-specific classification. Third, our dataset mainly comprises transcriptomic information. Further enhancement by the inclusion of proteomic or epigenetic profiling could expand the insights related to pathophysiologic alterations in glomerular disease. 57 Lastly, control tissues were obtained from histologically normal cortex of nephrectomy specimens rather than healthy donor biopsies; subtle transcriptional alterations from tumor microenvironment effects cannot be fully excluded. To minimize these effects, control samples were collected by intraoperative biopsy-gun before renal artery clamping, mimicking native biopsy acquisition. Future validation with living donor or preimplantation biopsies may further confirm disease-associated programs. In conclusion, we report an extensive snRNA-seq dataset generated from rare and clinically valuable treatment-naïve human kidney biopsy tissues across MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. This dataset uniquely captures disease-relevant transcriptomic states of kidney-resident cells at the time of diagnosis, offering a snapshot that is difficult to obtain in other models or settings. Our findings provide novel insights into disease- and cell type-specific alterations in glomerular diseases. As a resource study, this work constitutes a foundational reference atlas that may support future investigations aiming to discover diagnostic markers, therapeutic targets, and mechanistic pathways in human kidney disease. Importantly, because the KORNERSTONE cohort is primarily composed of Korean patients, this dataset also expands the ethnic diversity of currently available kidney single-cell reference resources, which remain heavily weighted toward Western populations. evidence_text:
Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal that the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis drives the immune-desert phenotype in small cell lung cancer by recruiting immunosuppressive CXCR4<sup>+</sup> neutrophils and S100A8<sup>+</sup> monocytes.

Background

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a recalcitrant malignancy with limited responses to immunotherapy, largely due to its uniquely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). However, the molecular mechanisms driving this phenotype remain incompletely understood.

Methods

We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics to analyze the immune microenvironment of five SCLC and four non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) samples. Multiplex immunofluorescence was used to validate cell types and gene expression in the same tissue specimens, and animal models were employed to verify the key mechanistic pathway.

Results

SCLC displayed a distinct immune landscape compared with NSCLC, with increased infiltration of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4)+ neutrophils (via neutrophil extracellular traps) and S100A8+ monocytes (toward an M2-like phenotype), and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Malignant epithelial cells in SCLC highly expressed CXCR4, regulated by transcription factors ISL LIM homeobox 1 and distal-less homeobox 5, which promoted immunosuppression. The C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)-CXCR4 axis mediated competitive inhibition, impairing T-cell recruitment while enhancing neutrophil accumulation. Monocytes in SCLC shifted toward an M2-like phenotype, weakening antigen presentation. Xenium spatial transcriptomics confirmed colocalization of CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes with tumor cells at the tumor-normal interface, while CD8+ T cells were spatially segregated. In vivo experiments showed that CXCR4 inhibition reduced SCLC tumor growth, decreased immunosuppressive cell infiltration, and enhanced CD8+ T-cell accumulation.

Conclusions

The CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, together with immunosuppressive CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes, is a key driver of the immune-desert phenotype in SCLC. Targeting this axis holds promise as a therapeutic strategy to remodel the immunosuppressive TME and improve the efficacy of immunotherapy for SCLC. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has a highly immunosuppressive “immune-desert” tumor microenvironment (TME) and poor immunotherapy response. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) show limited efficacy, but the spatial/cellular mechanisms driving the immune-desert phenotype remain unclear, hindering targeted therapy development. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS We delineate a mechanism by which the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)–C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) axis drives the SCLC immune desert. First, ISL LIM homeobox 1/distal-less homeobox 5-driven tumor cells secrete CXCL12. Second, this recruits immunosuppressive CXCR4 + neutrophils and S100A8 + M2-like monocytes, leading to CD8 + T-cell exclusion and impaired major histocompatibility complex-I expression. Finally, CXCR4 inhibition therapeutically reverses these effects, curtailing tumor growth and enhancing antitumor immunity. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This work provides a high-resolution SCLC TME map to guide CXCL12–CXCR4 research. Clinically, CXCR4 inhibitors may remodel TME and overcome ICI resistance. Practically, single-cell RNA sequencing/Xenium-based stratification can identify patients who benefit from CXCR4-targeted therapies, reducing ineffective treatment and advancing personalized care. Introduction Lung cancer (LC) has the highest global incidence and mortality. 1 Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) accounts for only approximately 15%–20% of all cases but is highly invasive with poor prognosis. 2 Although the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has improved therapeutic outcomes to some extent, the overall response rate remains relatively low. 3 Therefore, comprehensive research on the pathogenesis of SCLC and its complex immune microenvironment is urgently needed. However, the molecular regulatory network of SCLC is highly complex, involving dynamic imbalances in gene expression, dysregulation of epigenetic modifications, cross-talk among multiple signaling pathways, and intricate interactions between immunosuppressive cells and tumor cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), leading to limitations in subtyping accuracy and interpatient variability in treatment responses. 4 This complexity makes it challenging for analyses solely based on population-level molecular characteristics to comprehensively explain the mechanisms underlying SCLC initiation and progression and further complicates the accurate identification of potential therapeutic targets and drug resistance-related molecular events. Although ICIs have been incorporated into chemotherapy regimens in recent years, their clinical benefits remain limited. 5 From the perspective of the immune microenvironment, SCLC typically exhibits an immune-desert phenotype, characterized by extremely low infiltration of immune cells in the TME, low expression of immune checkpoint molecules, and frequent enrichment of fibrotic stroma and immunosuppressive cells, which together form a strong immunosuppressive barrier. 6 In contrast, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) frequently displays an immune-infiltrated phenotype, with infiltration of T and B cells and activation of immune checkpoint molecules in tumor tissues, suggesting active immune responses. 7 This distinction directly contributes to markedly different responses to immunotherapy between these two types of LC. The formation of the immune desert in SCLC may be related to the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells via chemokines secreted by tumor cells, whereas in the immune-infiltrated subtypes of NSCLC, immune escape more commonly relies on the activation of the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathway or T-cell exhaustion. Therefore, comparative studies on these two immune microenvironment subtypes may help reveal the specific mechanisms of immune escape in SCLC. The emergence of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology has provided a powerful approach to address these challenges. This method not only enables the resolution of transcriptomic profiles of immune, stromal, and tumor cells within the TME at single-cell resolution but also accurately identifies rare cell subpopulations that are undetectable by traditional bulk sequencing. 8 As an in situ spatial transcriptomic platform, Xenium enables subcellular, high-resolution spatial localization of hundreds of RNAs in intact tissues, allowing three-dimensional integrated analysis of “cellular phenotype–molecular characteristics–spatial location”. 9 The integration of scRNA-seq and Xenium not only precisely deciphers the gene expression profiles of individual cells but also defines their spatial context within the tissue. This combined approach holds promise for constructing a high-resolution single-cell atlas of the SCLC immune microenvironment, elucidating the cellular basis of immune desert formation, uncovering spatial interaction patterns between tumor cells and immune cell subsets, and identifying key signaling hubs that drive the development of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therefore, this study his study systematically dissected SCLC and NSCLC molecular characteristics via scRNA-seq/Xenium, characterized immune cell transcriptomes, validated spatial distribution via multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and verified key pathways in animal models to elucidate SCLC’s immune microenvironment and identify therapeutic targets. Results Global immune landscape in SCLC and NSCLC To comprehensively evaluate the immune landscape of SCLC, we collected nine tumor samples (five SCLC, four NSCLC) and performed scRNA-seq and in situ spatial transcriptomic analysis ( figure 1A ). After stringent filtering ( online supplemental Tables S1 and S2, Figure S1A-H ), 47,761 cells were obtained (24,133 NSCLC, 23,628 SCLC; figure 1B ), with 8 major cell types identified via marker genes: B cells (CD79A, JCHAIN), endothelial cells (CLDN5, CDH5), epithelial cells (EPCAM, KRT18), fibroblasts (DCN, PDGFRA), mast cells (CPA3, KIT), monocytes (LYZ, C1QA), neutrophils (CSF3R, FCGR3B), and T/NK cells (CD3D, NCAM1) ( figure 1C ). Cell cluster proportions were visualized ( figure 1D , S1I). χ 2 tests ( figure 1E ) and differential gene volcano plots ( online supplemental Figure S1J ) revealed significant differences in cell type composition between SCLC and NSCLC, with SCLC showing >twofold higher neutrophil proportion ( online supplemental Figure S1K ). Subset/marker expression was verified by scRNA-seq ( online supplemental Figure S1L ), and spatial distribution in tissue sections was examined via Xenium technology ( figure 1F , online supplemental Figure S2A and B ). Integrating Xenium and scRNA-seq data, we identified overlapping expressed genes, performed Pearson correlation analysis, and constructed heatmaps ( figure 1G , online supplemental Figure S2C ). Results showed significant consistency in cell type definition between the two methods, confirming Xenium’s reliability for studying LC cell composition and immune microenvironment. Differences in epithelial cells between NSCLC and SCLC result in distinct immune microenvironments From LC samples, 16,779 epithelial cells were isolated and divided into three subsets ( figure 2A ). Using stromal/macrophage cells as references, inferCNV analysis classified cells with mean square >0.05 and correlation coefficient >0.5 as malignant, identifying 12,628 malignant cells ( figure 2B , online supplemental Figure S3A-C ). Proportion statistics ( online supplemental Figure S3D ) and χ 2 tests ( figure 2C ) revealed differential distribution of the three malignant subsets between SCLC and NSCLC: C1 (predominantly SCLC), C2 (SCLC-2 specific), and C3 (predominantly NSCLC). Signature gene analysis showed C1 enriched for C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 ( CXCR4 ) and ISL LIM homeobox 1 ( ISL1 ), C2 for CDK6/HES5, and C3 for human leukocyte antigen ( HLA ) -A , HLA-B , and interferon-stimulated gene 15 ( ISG15 ) ( figure 2D ). In addition, SCLC also expressed ASCL1 , CD24 , CKB , CHGA , CXCR4 , TFF3 , ISL1 , and distal-less homeobox 5 ( DLX5 ) ( online supplemental Figure S3E ). Between SCLC and NSCLC, transcription factors ISL1/DLX5 were significantly activated in C1, with targets including CXCR4, suggesting SCLC may drive immune escape via ISL1-mediated CXCR4 overexpression. Differential gene analysis identified significantly upregulated CXCR4/ISL1 in SCLC ( figure 2E ). The results were visualized in a volcano plot ( figure 2F ), highlighting the top 20 upregulated and top 10 downregulated genes ( figure 2F ). Enrichment analysis showed SCLC upregulated genes linked to proliferation, drug resistance ( CKB ) 10 and endocrine function ( CHGA ), 11 while NSCLC upregulated genes related to TME immune regulation ( figure 2G ). Overlap between subset-specific signature genes and differentially expressed genes further validated subset functions. Quantitative set analysis for gene expression (QuSAGE) pathway analysis showed C1/C2 activated pathways associated with malignant progression (proliferation, mismatch repair, hypoxia), while C3 activated immune pathways (antigen presentation, natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity; figure 2H ), indicating NSCLC (C3) has stronger immune activity and SCLC (C1/C2) is immune-silent. SCENIC and differential gene analysis generated a ball-and-stick diagram. ISL1 was highly activated in C1, suggesting a key role in SCLC formation ( figure 2I ). Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( figure 2J , online supplemental Figure S4 ) and mIF staining ( figure 2K ) validated EPCAM + CXCR4 + cell distribution and expression. Xenium also verified some other key genes ( ASCL1, CHGA, CXCR4, ISL1 ; online supplemental Figure S4 ). In summary, important functional genes such as CXCR4 and ASCL1 are regulated by the same transcription factor, ISL1, which is a critical regulator of the neuroendocrine characteristics of SCLC, 12 whereas CXCR4 plays a pivotal role in tumor immune escape. 13 Figure 2 Proportion and distribution of CXCR4 + epithelial cells. CXCR4 + neutrophils mediate immunosuppression in SCLC Using scRNA-seq, we identified a substantial number of infiltrating neutrophils in SCLC. These neutrophils expressed classic markers (G0S2, FCGR3B) and high CXCR4 levels ( figure 3A,B , online supplemental Figure S5 ), leading us to hypothesize their role in competitive immunosuppression—analogous to CXCR4 + tumor cells that inhibit T-cell infiltration. Further analysis of differential gene expression (DGE) between SCLC and NSCLC neutrophils revealed alterations in ten core genes. CD74: impaired immune recognition 14 ; IL1R2: downregulation reduces inflammatory responsiveness 15 ; LGALS3: alters immune cell function 16 ; interleukin (IL)-1 receptor-associated kinase 3: disrupts immune signal transduction 17 ; endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 2: downregulation hinders T-cell recognition 18 ; IL-1 receptor antagonist: direct immunosuppression 19 ; protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type E: impairs immune activation 20 ; phosphodiesterase 4B: upregulation promotes tumor progression 21 ; prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2: upregulation aids angiogenesis/immune evasion 22 ; matrix metalloproteinase 25: upregulation favors invasion/metastasis ( figure 3C ). 23 Collectively, these alterations indicate suppression of immune-activating functions, ultimately leading to immune silence. Gene Ontology (GO)-Biological Process and pathway enrichment analysis showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory chemokines (IL-17, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)). Despite enhanced immune infiltration via strong chemokine binding, CXCR4 may bind C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to competitively inhibit immunity, downregulating phagocytosis/antigen presentation. Downregulation of ferroptosis/autophagy pathways weakened tumor cell death mediation ( figure 3D ). Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecule expression in neutrophils was significantly reduced in SCLC: violin plots showed lower HLA-A/B/C/E/F ( figure 3E ), and box plot scoring revealed impaired antigen presentation/CD8 + T-cell activation—indicating immunosuppressive effects. In NSCLC, MHC class I, type II interferons (IFNs), and immune responses correlated positively with CXCR4. This correlation was absent in SCLC ( figure 3F ), confirming SCLC neutrophils’ immunosuppressive state. Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics identified FCGR3B + neutrophils, confirming increased CXCR4 + neutrophil infiltration in SCLC and decreased IFIT3+/ISG15+neutrophils ( figure 3G , online supplemental Figure S6 ). mIF staining further validated these findings ( figure 3H ). Distribution and significance of monocytes in SCLC and NSCLC groups To explore immune microenvironment differences between SCLC and NSCLC, monocytes as a key immune cell subset were investigated. Using scRNA-seq and bioinformatics analysis, we identified four monocyte subtypes from the two groups ( figure 4A ), with their distribution visualized via Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction ( figure 4B ). Proportion statistics and χ 2 tests revealed significant intergroup differences: C2 and C3 proportions decreased, while C4 increased in SCLC ( figure 4C ). A bubble plot based on marker genes was used to further analyze the functional genes of each cell type. C1: FOLR2, highly expressed in specific macrophage subsets, links to macrophage activation and specialized phagocytosis. 24 It also expresses MHC class II molecules (HLA-DQA1, HLA-DPB1, HLA-DOA) for antigen presentation, which are critical for immune regulation by presenting antigenic peptides to CD4 + T cells and initiating adaptive immunity. 25 C2: MMP9 + macrophages. The expression of MMP9 suggests that these cells may participate in extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammation regulation. Enriched chemokine-related genes ( CSTB, CTSL, CCL2 ) mediate cell chemotaxis, guiding immune cell directional migration and regulating their distribution in the TME via binding to corresponding receptors. C3: ISG + monocytes. Enriched ISGs highlight their role in antiviral immunity and immune activation signaling. 26 IFN-related genes ( IFIT3, IFITM3, TNFSF10, ISG15 ) drive immune activation, enhancing host defense via JAK-STAT pathway activation to induce immune cell activation and cytokine secretion. 27 C4: S100A8 + monocytes. S100A8 associates with TME inflammation and tumor progression. 28 S100 family genes ( S100A4, S100A8 ) interact with intracellular/extracellular targets, activating pathways that promote tumor migration, invasion, and angiogenesis to drive progression. Comparative analysis confirmed C3 (ISG + monocytes) reduction and C4 (S100A8 + monocytes) increase in SCLC ( online supplemental Figure S7A,B ). Using QuSAGE bubble heatmaps, we systematically analyzed pathway enrichment across cell clusters. C1: Enriched in Th1/Th2 differentiation, phagosome formation, and antigen processing/presentation—key for immune cell activation, immune polarization (Th1/Th2 balance), and adaptive immunity initiation. C2/C3: Enriched in Nuclear Factor-kappa B (NF-κB) signaling, toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, cytokine–cytokine receptor interactions, and IL-17 signaling. These drive inflammation (NF-κB/TLR) and immune cell recruitment/activation (cytokine interactions, IL-17). 29 C4: Enriched in Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1 (HIF-1) signaling, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) signaling, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, which are critical for tumor hypoxia adaptation, angiogenesis (HIF-1/VEGF), and immune/inflammation regulation (NETs) ( online supplemental Figure S7C ). 30 The major expanded population in SCLC, C4, comprises S100A + FCN1 + monocytic cells. With weak antigen-presenting/phagocytic functions but activated VEGF/HIF pathways, C4 has strong vascular growth-promoting capacity, supporting its role in SCLC angiogenesis and progression. Among all cell types, monocytes had the highest neutrophil chemotactic factor (NCF) score, indicating the strongest neutrophil chemotaxis ( figure 4D ). SCLC exhibited stronger NCF activity, explaining its higher neutrophil infiltration. Violin plots of neutrophil chemokines showed notable changes in CXCL8 and CXCL5. Given CXCL8’s excessively high expression risked high background noise in Immunohistochemistry (IHC)/fluorescence staining, CXCL5 was selected for further analysis to highlight meaningful differences ( figure 4E ). Violin plot scoring showed lower MHC-I scores in SCLC ( figure 4F ), further validated by DGE volcano plots ( online supplemental Figure S7D ). Diminished MHC-I impairs antigen presentation, weakening CD8 + T-cell activation and anti-tumor immunity. Scoring plots and gene set heatmaps showed C3 had the highest M1-type molecule score and strongest M1-gene activation. Its reduction in SCLC reflected decreased M1-polarized macrophages. C4 (CXCR4 + immunosuppressive macrophages) increased in SCLC ( figure 4G ), indicating NSCLC features M1 polarization while SCLC shows M2 polarization. Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics confirmed CXCR4, CD163, CXCL5, IL1B, ISG15 expression in CD14 + monocytes, revealing SCLC monocytes are CXCL5 + (neutrophil-recruiting) and M2-polarized ( figure 3H , online supplemental Figure S8 ), further verified by mIF staining ( figure 3I ). Competitive immunosuppression leads to impaired infiltration of CD8+ T cells in SCLC CD8 + T cells are pivotal for dissecting LC pathogenesis and developing therapies. Distinct immune microenvironments in SCLC and NSCLC drive differences in CD8 + T-cell characteristics and functions. Exploring these differences is key to precise LC management. Here, scRNA-seq analysis of 5476 CD8 + T cells from LC samples characterized SCLC-specific CD8 + T-cell features, highlighting competitive inhibition by tumor cells. Single-cell clustering classified CD8 + T cells into effector memory T cell (Tem), T-cycling, exhausted T cell (Tex), effector T cell (Teff) (Temra), central memory T cell (Tcm), and SCLC/NSCLC-specific subgroups ( figure 5A and B ). Proportion analysis showed SCLC had increased Tcm/Teff but decreased Tex, Tem, T-cycling ( figure 5C , online supplemental Figure S9C ). Despite elevated Teff (high GNLY/GZMA) in SCLC, CD8 + T cells remained exhausted—likely due to high CXCR4 + tumor cells competing for immunoregulatory factors/cytokine binding sites/nutrients, inducing exhaustion and suppressing Teff activation/proliferation/infiltration. Reduced Tem/T-cycling Tex may result from tumor competitive inhibition, while decreased CD8 + T-cell infiltration lowers antigen/immunosuppressive factor exposure, contributing to Tex decline. To further investigate the genetic changes underlying these phenomena, we performed differential expression analysis of the gene expression profiles of CD8 + T cells between SCLC and NSCLC ( figure 5D–F , S9A). Volcano plots showed SCLC CD8 + T cells had upregulated immune checkpoint genes (eg, HAVCR2, TIGIT )—linked to enhanced exhaustion—and downregulated antigen recognition and signal transduction genes (eg, CD3, CD8 )—indicating impaired antigen presentation ( figure 5H ). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis revealed SCLC-enriched CD8 + T-cell cytotoxicity/exhaustion gene sets but downregulated T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling/activation sets ( figure 5G,H ). This may reflect high tumor CXCR4 expression: CXCR4 competes with CD8 + TCRs for chemokine binding, disrupting migration/TCR signaling and inhibiting activation. Additionally, tumor competitive inhibition may modulate monocytes via paracrine effects, downregulating MHC-I and further impairing CD8 + T-cell tumor recognition/elimination. Xenium in situ analysis of SCLC CD8 + T cells showed fewer T cell-enriched areas than tumor-infiltrated regions ( figure 5H , online supplemental Figure S10 ). T cells rarely entered the tumor core—consistent with ineffective immunity, as Teff failed to penetrate. Tumor cell proliferation and microenvironment remodeling spatially restricted CD8 + T-cell migration. High CXCR4 expression reshaped chemokine gradients, disrupting T-cell chemokine sensing/response and hindering tumor migration. mIF staining further validated CD8 + T-cell expression/distribution, S, which demonstrated that T cells in SCLC were reduced and exhibited exhaustion ( figure 5J ). Activation of the CXCL12–CXCR4 axis promotes SCLC immunosuppressive TME Cell–cell communication analysis revealed SCLC/NSCLC malignant cell differences ( figure 6A ): SCLC tumor cells linked to CXCL signaling, while NSCLC tumor cells were not. Further investigation of the key chemokine CXCL12 and its receptor CXCR4 showed NSCLC tumor cells neither produced nor responded to CXCL12, whereas SCLC tumor cells responded to CXCL12 stimulation ( figure 6B ). This difference is likely the primary driver of SCLC tumor cell competitive inhibition and is closely linked to SCLC metastasis. Pathway contribution analysis identified top three SCLC genes: GALECTIN, SPP1, CXCL . Among these, CXCL12/CXCR4 (T-cell infiltration-related) was downregulated (consistent with reduced T cells), CXCL8/CXCR2 (neutrophil-related) upregulated (aligning with increased neutrophils; figure 6C ). Ligand-receptor ranking showed SCLC upregulated CXCL8–CXCR2 and downregulated CXCL12–CXCR4, with distinct top pairs in NSCLC ( figure 6D ). Spatial distribution analysis showed NSCLC tumor epithelial cells and CD8 + T cells were fully intermingled without clear separation, whereas SCLC displayed a distinctly opposite distribution pattern for these two cell types. Similarly, CXCR4 + neutrophils showed a similar spatial trend ( figure 6E ). mIF staining further confirmed these findings ( figure 6F ). This spatial difference indicates a mutual inhibitory relationship between SCLC tumor and immune cells. CXCL12 stimulation may alter SCLC migration/microenvironment remodeling, spatially restricting immune cells, hindering tumor recognition/cytotoxicity, and forming a tumor-permissive TME.
