Breast and prostate cancers display complementary paradigms of malignant transition, with breast cancer driven by loss of suppressive regulators (MGP and PLAT) that restrain ECM remodeling and prostate cancer sustained by upregulation of oncogenic effectors (GDF15, ALDH1A3, ANPEP, and FASN) that promote metabolic reprogramming, stemness, and invasive capacity. Functional assays reveal that these opposing alterations converge on a shared outcome, namely enhanced proliferation and migration. Discussion In this study, we presented a comprehensive framework for understanding the spatial dynamics of tumor progression in breast and prostate cancers that share several commonalities. Leveraging a multimodal 3D serial section workflow, complemented by lightsheet microscopy, we identified key mechanisms underlying the transition from normal epithelial, precancer, to invasive epithelial cell states. By integrating transcriptomics, multiplex imaging, and histologic staining, we moved beyond the inherent limitations of traditional 2D analyses to provide a unified view of tumor architecture and TME interactions across three dimensions and in the context of spatially defined gene expression patterns. Despite these advances, full integration across spatial platforms remains challenging due to differences in assay resolution, gene coverage, and sampling density, which may limit the consistency of feature detection across datasets. In addition, intrinsic tissue heterogeneity presents a challenge for 3D reconstruction and downstream analyses, as spatially distinct regions within the same tissue can exhibit divergent gene expression trends, contributing to variability in correlations observed across ROIs and between cohort-level and ROI-level analyses. Furthermore, the generation of large-scale 3D spatial datasets remains time and cost intensive, necessitating the incorporation of complementary 2D sections to increase statistical power and support the robustness of identified transition-associated features. We show a native 3D view of intact breast and prostate tumor tissues with volumes on the order of ∼10 mm 3 by implementing advanced tissue clearing and lightsheet microscopy methodologies. The discovery of interconnected regions spanning millimeter-scale distances highlights the advantage of 3D analyses in understanding tumor topology and spatial relationships that would be missed by 2D imaging. In this study, we stained tumor samples with CK5 and PanCK to clearly distinguish precancerous lesions, invasive carcinoma, and adjacent normal structures, revealing that invasive carcinoma regions form an interconnected tree-like tumor structure in both cancers, despite being seemingly disconnected and scattered on a 2D section. Our native 3D imaging approach allows for a direct spatial visualization of intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity, as well as interactions between cancer cells and TME components. By tracing specific regions using a 3D serial sectioning approach, we were able to follow the neoplastic transition along continuous structures intersected with planes of spatial omics data, allowing a view into gene expression changes, a feat not possible with a 2D sectioning approach alone. We identified multiple 3D ROIs having transitional regions along the z axis. For example, we follow the transition of a prostate gland from normal, to HGPIN, to GP3 morphology, as well as a breast DCIS region through MI into the surrounding tissue and eventually into wholly invasive cells. Due to our approach of using different spatial platforms at strategic locations, we were able to trace these transitions with a variety of different high-dimensional sets of molecular features and cross-validate such features. With our integrated gene discovery approach, we highlight several key diverse and shared mechanisms driving the transition from normal to invasive epithelial cells, most of which are involved in four biological processes, including tissue integrity/ECM remodeling, cell–cell communications, metabolism/homeostasis, as well as proliferation and survival ( Fig. 6B ). Accumulating evidence indicates that microcalcification in the context of breast cancer can be proinvasive ( 71 , 72 ). We identified MGP , a gene not previously known in DCIS-to-IDC transition, whose primary function is to prevent calcium deposition by directly binding Ca 2+ and also by binding BMP2 and not allowing BMP2 signal to be transduced downstream ( 73 – 75 ). At the same time, BMP2 has been shown to induce EMT and promote metastasis in breast cancer models ( 76 ), which suggests why the loss of its inhibitor might be beneficial for invasive cancer. We also identify PLAT as common to both the prostate and breast transition and implicated in tissue remodeling. Additionally, we find genes that differ in their expression patterns between breast and prostate invasive cells, such as ANPEP and ALDH1A3 (overexpressed in prostate and underexpressed in breast). Furthermore, we identify shared markers, such as FASN and EPHA6 , that are both overexpressed in invasive areas across both cancer types. Although many of the transition-associated genes are different between breast and prostate cancers, reflecting tissue specificity, the commonalities in the biological processes affected may indicate the key events required for cancers with glandular luminal cell origins to initiate and progress. Both DCIS and PIN are precancerous lesions trapped inside a ductal network with basal cells, basement membranes, and surrounding stromal components restricting their movement. Changes in proliferation/survival and metabolism inside the breast and prostate luminal cells are key for the intrinsic neoplastic transition and alterations in genes involved in tissue integrity/ECM remodeling and cell–cell communications are critical for the progression into more aggressive growth (IDC and PCa) outside of the confines of the ductal/glandular structures and in a completely different microenvironment with many more cells to interact with and signals to respond to. It is worth noting that several of these genes involved in the transitions, especially those shared between prostate and breast cancers, are hormone-regulated genes, including MYC , GDF15 , and FASN . Estrogen directly upregulates MYC ( 77 ) in breast cancer, whereas in prostate cancer, androgen signaling can increase MYC expression ( 78 ). Similarly, both estrogens and androgens regulate FASN expression in several cancer types, including breast and prostate cancers ( 79 , 80 ). Conversely, products of some of these genes can also modulate hormone signaling ( 81 ). In addition, some of the genes found uniquely in either cancer are also regulated by hormones. For example, androgen upregulates ALDH1A3 in prostate cancer cells ( 82 ). The precise mechanism of hormonal regulation of these genes and the potential reciprocal impact on hormonal signaling in the context of tumor transition remains to be elucidated. Furthermore, our analysis of the TME emphasizes the dynamic contributions of TAMs and CAFs to invasive transition. The spatial segregation of SPP1 + and MS4A6A + TAMs suggests that these macrophage populations may differentially support progression depending on tumor subtype. Whereas SPP1 + TAMs have been broadly implicated in tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive functions ( 83 – 85 ), our data indicate a nuanced role in progression, with enrichment specifically at invasive fronts in non-TNBC breast cancers but not in TNBC breast or prostate tumors. In contrast, MS4A6A + TAMs, previously observed in glioma and breast ( 84 , 86 , 87 ), were associated with noninvasive regions, indicating a role slowing invasive transition. Similarly, CAFs with expression of MFAP5 and ASPN were enriched around invasive regions, indicating their known roles in matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and activation of pro-EMT signaling could be affecting invasive transition ( 54 – 56 , 58 , 59 ). Together, these findings support that epithelial invasion is not solely driven by tumor-intrinsic programs but also by specific TAM and CAF populations. The challenges of precisely defining precancerous states have now come to the forefront because of its immediate relevance to recognizing which cases will progress to full malignancy and when medical and/or surgical treatment should be commenced ( 88 ). Although changes like somatic mutations and epigenetic modifications can now be discerned, these alone do not paint a sufficiently specific picture for initiating clinical intervention. The approach developed here and the subsequent findings should contribute to better defining precancerous states across cancer types by further refining hallmarks, including spatial characteristics of cancer-related pathways and genes, telltale tissue remodeling patterns, and signals from the ECM and TME. The ability to distinguish what are essentially substeps along the normal-to-malignant continuum and the subsequent translation of same to the clinic should materially improve protocols for early intervention, which is still viewed as the option in which the greatest medical benefit can be provided to the patient ( 89 ). Methods Specimens and Sample Processing All samples were collected with written informed consent from patients at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis [Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol 201108117]. All studies were conducted in accordance with recognized ethical guidelines, including the Declaration of Helsinki, CIOMS guidelines, and the US Common Rule, and were approved by the IRB. After tumor identification, each portion was subdivided into multiple pieces which were then further divided into four transverse-cut pieces. These four pieces were then each respectively placed into a combination of formalin, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and DMEM and snap-frozen before embedding in optimal cutting temperature (OCT). Relevant protocols can be found at protocols.io ( https://doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bszynf7w ). Visium Library Preparation and Sequencing Visium sections were generated using protocols reported previously ( 90 – 92 ). Specifically, for OCT-embedded samples, detailed methods have been described by Zhou and colleagues ( 91 ), whereas methods for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples are described in Wu and colleagues ( 92 ). Briefly, OCT-embedded tissue or FFPE tissue samples were sectioned and placed on a Visium Spatial Gene Expression Slide following the Visium Spatial Protocols–Tissue Preparation Guide. For OCT, fresh tissue samples were coated with room temperature OCT and then sectioned (10 μm). Sections were then fixed in methanol, stained with H&E, and imaged at 20× magnification using the brightfield imaging setting on a Leica DMi8 microscope. Tissue samples were then permeabilized for 18 minutes, and ST libraries were constructed following the Visium Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kit user guide CG000239 (10x Genomics). For FFPE tissues, quality assessment was performed using the Visium Tissue Section Test Slide, along with an RNA quality check following the Visium Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE–Tissue Preparation Guide CG000408 (10x Genomics). Blocks were scored and sectioned to fit in the capture areas of the Visium Spatial Gene Expression Slide. Deparaffinization, H&E staining, and decrosslinking were performed following CG000409 (10x Genomics). ST libraries were constructed following Visium Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE user guide CG000407 (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on a S4 flow cell of an Illumina NovaSeq-6000 system. Relevant protocols for ST for FFPE utilizing 10x Genomics Visium (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.kxygx95ezg8j/v1) and ST for OCT using 10x Genomics Visium (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.x54v9d3opg3e/v1) can be found on protocols.io. Visium Data Processing For each sample, we obtained the unfiltered feature–barcode matrix per sample by passing the demultiplexed FASTQ files and associated H&E image to Space Ranger (v.1.3.0, v.2.0.0 and v2.1.0 “count” command using default parameters with reorient-images enabled) and the prebuilt GRCh38 genome reference 2020-A (GRCh38 and Ensembl 98). Visium HD Library Preparation and Sequencing FFPE tissue samples were sectioned and placed onto a standard, charged glass slide following the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Guide CG000684 (10x Genomics). Following hybridization and ligation, the probes were released from the 5-μm sections and captured by Visium HD Slide (10x Genomics, 1000670) using the Visum CytAssist instrument (10x Genomics, 1000499). The standard workflow was followed for downstream library processing using the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent User Guide CG000685 (10x Genomics). Barcoded libraries were then sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 system with associated flow cells to a targeted run size of at least 250 mol/L read pairs. Visium HD Data Processing For each sample, we obtained the unfiltered feature–barcode matrix per sample by passing the demultiplexed FASTQ files, associated H&E image, and CytAssist image to Space Ranger (v2.1.0 “count” command using default parameters with reorient-images enabled) and the prebuilt GRCh38 genome reference 2020-A (GRCh38 and Ensembl 98). Xenium Data Generation FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm and placed on Xenium slides following a modified version of the FFPE Tissue Preparation Guide (10x Genomics, CG000578 , Rev B). Slides were deparaffinized via a series of xylene and ethanol washes prior to decrosslinking utilizing the FFPE tissue enhancer as described (10x Genomics, CG000580 , Rev B). Overnight in situ probe hybridization was performed utilizing Human Multi-Tissue and Cancer Panel (10x Genomics, 1000626) of probes for 377 genes. Selected panels received an additional custom panel of probes for extra 100 genes (Supplementary Table S5). Probes were subsequently ligated and underwent rolling circle amplification. The background was quenched using an autofluorescence mixture. Nuclei were stained with DAPI to improve on-instrument sample tracking and cell boundary segmentation (10x Genomics, CG000582 , Rev D). Samples were then loaded onto the 10X Xenium Analyzer instrument (10x Genomics, 1000481) for imaging and initial data processing following the manufacturer’s instructions (10x Genomics, CG000584 , Rev C). H&E staining of the post-Xenium slide was performed after the run following the provided guidance (10X Genomics, CG000613 , rev B). Relevant protocols for 10x Genomics Xenium for FFPE User Guides (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.81wgbxjonlpk/v1) can be found on protocols.io. Xenium Prime (5K) Data Generation FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm and mounted onto Xenium slides following a modified version of the FFPE Tissue Preparation Guide (10x Genomics, CG000578 , Rev D). Slides were deparaffinized with sequential xylene and ethanol washes, followed by decrosslinking using the FFPE Tissue Enhancer and diluted Perm Enzyme B (10x Genomics, CG000580 , Rev E). Xenium Prime predesigned and add-on custom priming oligos were hybridized to target RNAs in situ . After RNase treatment to release the RNA strand, a polishing step was performed, followed by overnight probe hybridization utilizing the Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (10x Genomics, 1000724) of probes for 5001 genes and an additional custom panel of probes for extra 100 genes (Supplementary Table S5). Probes were subsequently ligated and underwent rolling circle amplification, generating multiple copies of the gene-specific barcode for each RNA target. Cell segmentation reagents were applied during a staining workflow to label nuclei, membranes, and cytoplasmic regions for automated morphology-based segmentation. The background was quenched using an autofluorescence mixture, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI to aid in sample tracking and cell boundary segmentation (10x Genomics, CG000760 , Rev C). Xenium slides were then loaded onto the 10X Xenium Analyzer instrument (10x Genomics, 1000481) for imaging and initial data processing following the manufacturer’s instructions (10x Genomics, CG000584 , Rev F). Fluorescently labeled oligos bind to the amplified DNA probes, and iterative rounds of probe hybridization, imaging, and stripping generated optical signatures for each barcode, which were decoded to gene identities. The H&E staining of the post-Xenium slides was performed after the run following the guidance provided (10X Genomics, CG000613 , Rev B). CosMx Sample Preparation and Data Generation CosMx SMI profiling was carried out on breast and prostate tumor FFPE blocks, ID HT704B1-S1H3Fp1 and HT891Z1-S2H3Fp1, using CosMx 1K and 6K Discovery Panel respectively. FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm thickness and placed on VWR Superfrost Plus Micro slides. Slides were deparaffinized via a couple of xylene and ethanol washes prior to heat-induced target retrieval at 100°C for 15 minutes using 1× Target Retrieval Solution. The tissue sections were digested using 5 µg/mL Proteinase K incubated at  40°C for 30 minutes in a hybridization chamber. Slides were washed twice with 1× PBS and incubated in 0.0004% fiducials diluted in 2× SSCT for 5 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Excess fiducials were rinsed from the slides with 1× PBS and tissue sections were fixed with 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) for 1  minute at room temperature. Fixed samples were rinsed twice with Stop Buffer, composed of 0.1  mol/L glycine and 0.1  mol/L Tris-base in DEPC H 2 O, and once with 1× PBS for 5 minutes each before blocking with 100 mmol/L NHS acetate in CosMX NHS acetate buffer (Bruker Spatial Biology) for 15 minutes at room temperature. The sections were then rinsed with 2× SSC for 5 minutes and incubated with hybridization solution (Denatured CosMx RNA Probe mixes) on the hybridization chamber at 37°C for 18 hours. After 18 hours, washes with stringent solution (50% formamide in 2× SSC) and 2× SSC buffer were performed to rinse of excess probes. Nuclear staining was carried out for 15 minutes in the dark in the hybridization chamber, and slides were washed with 1× PBS to remove excess stain. Cell segmentation was carried using cell segmentation mix (CD292/B2M), marker mix (PanCK/CD45), and a la carte mix (CD68) for 1 hour at room temperature in the hybridization chamber and the samples were rinsed thrice with 1× PBS and twice with 2× SSC. The Flow cells with unique barcodes were assembled on the slides, which were then loaded on CosMx SMI, running on software v1.3.1, following instructions provided in CosMx SMI Instrument User Manual (Man-10161-02-1). The Raw data and flatfiles generated were downloaded from the AtoMx platform for subsequent analysis following the manufacturer’s guidelines. https://github.com/Nanostring-Biostats/CosMxDACustomModules . Tissue Clearing, Staining, and Imaging for 3D Lightsheet Tissue was obtained through the WU Solid Tumor Tissue Bank from surgical patients after written informed consent with the aid of an attending pathologist. Briefly, each tissue block is documented by photographing, weighing, and recording a description of anatomical landmarks and is further subdivided up into 4 to 6 smaller tissue blocks. Each of the smaller blocks is then subdivided into three pieces approximately 6 mm × 6 mm × 2 mm each and processed as follows: 1) 10% NBF for histologic characterization, e.g. H&E and CODEX; 2) snap-freezing in liquid nitrogen or embedding in OCT for genomic analysis; and 3) fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde for lightsheet. The piece that is designated for lightsheet is washed in PBS after 24 hours and is then ready for tissue clearing. For tissue clearing, samples were firstly infiltrated with SHIELD polyepoxy ( 93 ) for 6 days with constant agitation at 4 C, subsequently polymerized at 37°C for 24 hours, and then delipidated using a SmartBatch+ ETC active tissue clearing platform (LifeCanvas Technologies). Samples were washed in 1× PBS for 24 hours at room temperature before proceeding to antibody staining and were permeabilized with 1× PBS containing 0.2% Triton X-100 twice for one hour each at room temperature before blocking. Samples were blocked with 6% donkey serum at 37°C with PBS containing 0.2% Triton X-100 and 10% DMSO. After blocking, samples were washed with PBS containing 0.2% Tween-20 plus 10 µg/mL heparin twice at 37°C and then incubated with fluorescently conjugated antibodies for 4 days at 37°C. Antibodies included AF488-conjugated anti-CK5 (AB_2893023) and AF594-conjugated anti-PanCK (AB_3741555). All antibodies were diluted at 1:200 in PBS containing 0.2% Tween-20, 5% DMSO, 3% donkey serum, and 10 µg/mL heparin. On day 3, Hoechst was added to the solution at 1:10,000. After staining, samples were washed at least 5 times in PBS/0.2% Tween-20/10 µg/mL heparin, exchanging the solution every 1 hour. After staining, samples were refractive index–matched to 1.52 using EasyIndex RI matching media (LifeCanvas Technologies). Whole-sample images were acquired on a Miltenyi Ultra Microscope Blaze Gaussian lightsheet platform using a 4×/0.35 MI PLAN objective. Datasets were stitched together using Stitchy (Translucence Biosystems) and visualized using Bitplane Imaris 10.1.1 (Oxford Instruments). The lateral resolution of lightsheet microscopy can be estimated as the emission wavelength divided by two times the numerical aperture, yielding 0.741 μm for the CK5 channel and 0.881 μm for the PanCK channel. Because the structures of interest do not require sampling at the theoretical resolution limit, we used a lateral sampling interval of 1.62 μm. The axial resolution of our FLSM setup is determined by the thickness of the light sheet (7 μm) and was sampled at the Nyquist frequency. CODEX Preparation and Imaging Carrier-free monoclonal or polyclonal anti-human antibodies were purchased (Supplementary Table S4) and verified using IF staining in multiple channels. After the screening, antibodies were conjugated using the Akoya Antibody Conjugation Kit (Akoya Biosciences, SKU 7000009) with a specific barcode (Akoya Biosciences) assigned according to the IF staining results. Several common markers were directly purchased through Akoya Biosciences. Keyence protocol: CODEX staining and imaging were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (CODEX User Manual - Rev C). Briefly, 5 μm FFPE sections were placed on APTES (Sigma, #440140) coated coverslips and baked at 60°C overnight before deparaffinization. The next day, tissues were incubated in xylene, rehydrated in ethanol, and washed in ddH2O before antigen retrieval with TE buffer, pH 9 (Genemed, #10-0046), in boiling water for 10 minutes in a rice cooker. The tissues were then blocked using the blocking buffer (CODEX staining kit SKU 7000008) and stained with the marker antibody panel to a volume of 200 µL for 3 hours at room temperature in a humidified chamber. Imaging of the CODEX multicycle experiment was performed using a Keyence fluorescence microscope (model BZ-X810) equipped with a Nikon CFI Plan Apo λ 20x/0.75 objective, the CODEX instrument (Akoya Biosciences), and CODEX Instrument Manager (CIM; Akoya Biosciences). The raw images were then stitched and processed using the CODEX processor (Akoya Biosciences). After multiplex imaging was completed, H&E staining was performed on the same tissue. Panels for each codex section are listed in Supplementary Table S4. Phenocycler protocol: The immunostaining procedure was conducted using the PhenoCycler-Fusion sample kit (Akoya, cat. #7000017) following Akoya’s user guide. Selected FFPE samples were sectioned at 5 μm thickness, placed on charged slides (Fisherbrand, cat. #1255015), and dried at 42°C on a heat block. Prior to deparaffinization, the slides were baked at 65°C overnight. Deparaffinization was done using two times Xylene followed by rehydration in a graded series of ethanol (two times 100%, 90%, 70%, 50%, and 30%) and two times Milli-Q water (ddH2O). Antigen retrieval was performed for prostate cancer in 1× Tris-EDTA (pH 9) using a rice cooker for 18 minutes, and for breast cancer tissue for 20 minutes. After equilibrating to room temperature, sample slides were washed twice in the hydration buffer and then equilibrated in the staining buffer for 30 minutes. Subsequently, slides were incubated with all antibodies diluted in 200 µL staining buffer containing N Blocker, G Blocker, J Blocker, and S Blocker for 3 hours at room temperature in a humidified chamber. After staining, slides were washed twice in the staining buffer and fixed with 1.6% paraformaldehyde in the storage buffer for 10 minutes. Samples slides are then washed three times in PBS and incubated in ice-cold methanol for 5 minutes, followed by three times washes in PBS and incubation in the final fixative solution for 20 minutes. After three additional PBS washes, slides were stored in a storage buffer for a maximum of 3 days before imaging. The reporters were prepared following Akoya’s PhenoCycler-Fusion user guide and dispensed into a 96-well black plate. The experimental template for the PhenoCycler-Fusion Run was designed using Akoya’s PhenoCycler Experiment Designer software. Details about antibodies used for each codex run are available in Supplementary Table S4. The experimental run was executed using Akoya’s Fusion 1.0.8, and final images were generated on the PhenoImager Fusion microscope using default settings. 3D Serial Sectioning Procedure FFPE blocks were chilled on ice for at least 20 minutes before sectioning. Tissue was cut at a thickness of 5 μm to capture the full surface of the sample, continuing until the regions of interest were fully included. Once the optimal surface exposure and section quality were achieved, tissue ribbons were cut continuously until the tissue was exhausted or the required number of sections was obtained. The sections were labeled sequentially (U1, U2, U3, etc.) during the sectioning process. Upon completing the sectioning, the ribbons were gently placed on a clean surface and divided into smaller ribbons, each consisting of 8 to 10 sections. These smaller ribbons were slowly transferred to a water bath, ensuring they floated in a line without folds or breaks. Any section that folded or broke prior to slide mounting was discarded, whereas its section number was retained. The sections were carefully loaded one by one onto regular glass slides, Visium slides, or Xenium slides in the planned sequence. Subsequently, the slides were processed according to spatial platform–specific protocols. Section retention for each sample can be viewed in Supplementary Table S7. 3D Serial Section Registration Prior to registration, imaging data underwent the following transformations. Multiplex, Xenium, and CosMx images were converted to grayscale images of the nuclear intensity channel. The images were then downscaled by a factor of 5 before key point selection. For Visium and Visium HD, H&E images (also downsampled by a factor of 5) were used for keypoint selection. For registration, we used the BigWarp tool (arXiv:1511.01154), which was packaged in the Fiji/ImageJ software application. To register each collection of serial images, we use the first serial section as the fixed image and the second image as the moving image. After the second image is warped to the first image, the second image is used as the fixed image for the transformation of the third image. Key point registration proceeds in this fashion for all images in the serial section experiment. A total of 4 to 10 key points were selected per image transformation. Once key points were selected, a moving field was exported from BigWarp for each image transformation (thin plate spline). This dense displacement field (DDF) was then upscaled by a factor of 5 so it could be used to warp the full-resolution image data. The DDF was then also used to register corresponding point-based data (transcript locations for CosMx and Xenium, spot locations for Visium, and grid locations for Visium HD). The code used for registration is available at https://github.com/ding-lab/mushroom/blob/main/README.md#manuscript-materials . Breast 3D Connectivity Analysis We constructed 3D region volumes to analyze connectivity of serial section breast cancer cases (HT704B1, HT206B1, and HT397B1) using Xenium, CODEX, and H&E sections in a three-part process: (i) protein abundance prediction from H&E slides, (ii) automated epithelial region annotation, and (iii) interconnected region reconstruction. Due to gaps between Xenium and CODEX sections, we decided to fill in these gaps using H&E sections. Because H&E has no inherent marker for epithelial cells, we trained a deep learning model to predict marker abundance using H&E as input. To enable volumetric reconstruction of epithelial connectivity across serial sections, we used a deep learning model to approximate epithelial marker abundance in intervening H&E sections. This model was used exclusively for epithelial region segmentation to support 3D connectivity analysis. For training, we used an adjacent CODEX and H&E section to train a separate model for each of the three serial section cases. At inference time, the input to the model was an H&E section, and the output was protein abundance for certain CODEX markers (Supplementary Table S8). Model architecture, training methodology, and inference time mechanics are described below. Architecture and training parameters can be found in Supplementary Table S8. We use a U-net (arXiv:1505.04597) with a ResNet-18 backbone (arXiv:1512.03385, arXiv:2110.00476) followed by a prediction head composed of 2D convolutions for protein abundance prediction. We train a separate model for each case. For training, we select adjacent CODEX and H&E sections. The images are preprocessed in the following manner. First, each channel of the H&E and CODEX image is normalized by mean and standard deviation. Natively, these images are too large to pass through the model, so they must be tiled for training and inference. As such, we shred each image into 256 × 256 pixel tiles. However, when using tiles we remove the morphologic context of the area outside the tile that may be useful for protein abundance prediction. Appending additional regional context to a tile is one way to remedy this issue ( 94 ). To give each tile context of morphology outside its immediate surroundings, we also train additional Unets in parallel with their input being zoomed-out, low resolution (2×, 4×, 8×, and 16×) views centered on the given tile. After the forward pass through each Unet, the resulting activations are then concatenated prior to input into the prediction head. With this procedure, we are able to give each high-resolution tile regional morphologic context helpful to protein prediction. The model was implemented using the Pytorch Python library (arXiv:1912.01703). During training, we randomly select image tiles from a uniform distribution across the 2D section. Each tile is then horizontally or vertically flipped with 50% probability. Most serial H&E sections were imaged in the same batch to minimize batch effects across slides. As such, we did not perform other color-based image augmentations to the input image tiles. Following the forward pass through the Unet and prediction head, we are left with a C × W × H tensor in which height and width are the same shape as the input image tile and c is the number of CODEX proteins being predicted. For model loss, we use mean squared error (MSE) between the predicted values and the ground truth protein abundance, in which the ground truth values are the protein abundance in the CODEX section adjacent to the H&E section. Each model was trained for 640,000 steps with a batch size of 64. Following training, we performed model inference over all H&E serials sections, which generated protein abundance values for every H&E section. We then used expression of epithelial marker genes to identify epithelial regions (encompassing normal, DCIS, and IDC morphology) in an automated fashion. First, we selected epithelial marker genes for each sample based on what genes and proteins were available in a given Xenium or CODEX panel. First, we tiled all inputs to a resolution of 15 μm per pixel. To tile Xenium data, the area covered by the Xenium section was split into 15-µm grid squares. We then summed the aggregate expression counts of all cells within each grid square. For CODEX and H&E, we rescaled the images to a resolution of 15 μm per pixel. We selected a 15-µm tiling resolution because the primary objective was region-level epithelial segmentation. Given minor registration uncertainty and occasional missing serial sections, volumetric continuity is fundamentally constrained by z-axis sampling density rather than in-plane resolution. The 15-µm resolution provided an appropriate balance between epithelial segmentation accuracy and consistency with intersection spacing. A cutoff value was then defined via manual inspection for each of these markers in a case-independent fashion. The cutoff value was then applied in the following way to segment epithelial regions. First, all pixels with a value greater than the cutoff value were considered epithelial pixels. Then a binary hole filling algorithm was applied to fill holes in regions, for this we use the scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes function from the scipy Python package (arXiv:1907.10121). Interconnected areas of epithelial pixels were then identified by constructing a N × H × W array in which N is the total number of Xenium, CODEX, and H&E sections for a case. Each voxel was either positive (epithelial) or negative (nonepithelial). Adjacent epithelial voxels were considered connected. We used the skimage.morphology.label function from the scikit-image Python package ( 95 ) to then identify connected 3D regions. Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions We use manual region annotation to label interconnected epithelial regions for connectivity analysis and 3D ROI path construction. First, we generate an OME-TIFF for each region of interest. The OME-TIFF stores a stack of pseudo-color images representing each serial section. The OME-TIFF was then viewed with the QuPath ( 96 ) image viewing platform. Manual epithelial region annotation was then performed in QuPath. Annotated region coordinates were then exported in GeoJSON format ( https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946 ) for downstream visualization and analysis. Selection and Annotation of 3D Serial Section ROIs ROIs were selected based on areas of region morphology. Searching for interconnected morphology was conducted with the Imaris 3D image viewing platform. We generated pseudo-color images for each serial section as described in the manual annotation section above, with these images then being converted to an .ims file using Imaris, following which we were able to view each pseudo-color image to identify interconnected epithelial regions undergoing noninvasive to invasive transition (normal, HGPIN, and GP3 in prostate; DCIS, MI, and IDC in breast). Cross sections of these transitioning regions were then annotated using the approach described in “Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions” (Supplementary Tables S9 and S10). Gene Discovery Overview We selected ROIs that had interconnected noninvasive to invasive morphology. Each 2D cross section of the interconnected structure was segmented to enable tracing of the continuity and transitions between progression states, enabling a more detailed understanding of the spatial and molecular dynamics of the progression within a singular structure. This analysis would not be possible with traditional, nonserial 2D image sections. To identify genes differentially expressed in IDC compared with DCIS, we leveraged both 2D and 3D ST datasets (Xenium, CosMx, Visium, and Visium HD). For 2D cohort-level gene discovery, we used both automated and manual annotation methods on ST sections. Automated differential gene expression discovery was performed in Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD sections. This involved identifying epithelial regions and assessing myoepithelial intensity using basal layer markers, which were then correlated to gene expression (see “2D automated gene discovery”), allowing the identification of genes associated with myoepithelial integrity (Supplementary Table S11). To supplement the automated approach, we also implemented a manual workflow in which areas of DCIS ( n = 5+) and IDC ( n = 5+) morphology were randomly manually selected in Visium sections (Supplementary Table S12; see “2D manual gene discovery”). DEG identification was subsequently performed based on these manual annotations. For 3D ROI-level gene discovery, we identified DEGs specific to 3D ROIs to characterize gene expression changes across progression states within a single interconnected epithelial structure (Supplementary Tables S13 and S14). For 3D gene discovery, we use two approaches: morphology-based and path-based (see “3D gene discovery”). Briefly, for morphology-based, regions were annotated (DCIS, MI, or IDC in breast; normal, HGPIN, or GP3 in prostate) and expression differences between groups were quantified with the Student t test and fold change. In path-based discovery, regression was run on expression values for each region along the path of the transitioning epithelial structure. Together, this dual-layered approach provided a comprehensive view of the gene expression landscape, revealing key molecular pathways and biological processes involved in invasive transition. Manual curation and visual inspection further refined the identification of genes specific to luminal epithelial cells and linked to breast cancer progression. 2D Automated Gene Discovery We used both manual and automated methods for 2D DEG discovery. For automated discovery, we first annotated epithelial regions across Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD sections with invasive and noninvasive morphology in the dataset. For Xenium and CosMx, the process consisted of first tiling all inputs to the same resolution: 10 µm per pixel. We then identified epithelial regions in an automated fashion. First, all tiled sections were normalized by standard deviation at the gene level. An epithelial mask was then constructed by thresholding each grid for EPCAM >1.0. This mask was then run through a hole-filling algorithm to fill in gaps present due to transcript sparsity and necrosis. All positive grids (i.e., pixels) were considered epithelial pixels. We then used the skimage.morphology.label function from the scikit-image Python package ( 95 ) to identify areas of connected pixels. Interconnected pixels with a tiled area of less than 10 were filtered out. These remaining areas of pixels were considered epithelial regions. For Visium HD, we had two annotation methods based on the data available. For sections that were included in the 3D stacked serial section dataset, we used outputs from the U-net model from “Breast 3D Connectivity Analysis” as epithelial “expression”. We then generated epithelial masks in an identical manner to the previous paragraph. For Visium HD sections that were not part of the stacked 3D dataset, we underwent the same procedure as Xenium and CosMx with the following changes: the normalized expression image was Gaussian-blurred (alpha = 5), and EPCAM was thresholded at 0.1. The expression image was Gaussian-blurred to account for the additional sparsity introduced by tiling with 2-µm Visium HD squares. Following identification of regions, we quantified feature expression for three areas of the region: the region itself (i.e., luminal cells), the region boundary (i.e., basal layer), and the area surrounding the region (i.e., TME). Masks were generated to identify pixels belonging to each of these areas and were defined in the following ways. The “region” mask is the same as the epithelial mask previously described but shrank by 10 μm. The “boundary” mask was defined by the area between the epithelial mask and the epithelial mask expanded by 20 μm. The “TME” mask was defined by expanding the epithelial region 40 μm and subtracting the “boundary” and “region” masks. Region area masks were not allowed to expand into another region’s area. The skimage.segmentation.expand_labels function from the scikit-image ( 95 ) Python package was used to expand epithelial regions. Expression was then quantified for each region, boundary, and TME mask. With expression values in hand, we were able to correlate feature expression within regions (“region” mask) to boundary (“boundary” mask) expression of basal layer markers. A positive correlation value for a feature in a section indicates that for regions within that section, intra-region expression of that gene is associated with higher expression of basal layer markers in the region boundary (i.e., the genes expression is associated with regions having a more intact basal cell layer). Negative correlations indicate the opposite association. The same metric was also obtained for the area outside regions (“TME” mask) in order to identify TME genes associated with region basal layer expression. We defined the TME as the peritumoral region extending 100 µm from the epithelial boundary. This distance captures stromal and immune cells within biologically relevant interaction range of tumor epithelium, consistent with spatial oncology studies that define cellular neighborhoods on the scale of tens to hundreds of μm ( 97 – 99 ). A 100-µm margin balances inclusion of the immediate invasive niche while minimizing incorporation of distant stromal regions unlikely to directly influence epithelial transition. Due to marker absence in panels between and within spatial platforms, the same basal layer marker could not be used for every section. The basal layer marker for a section was determined by selecting a gene out of the following list of markers: ( KRT5 , KRT14 , KRT15 , LAMB3 , and ACTA2 ). For each sample, we iterated through the marker list, and once a basal marker gene was found to be in that sample, we used that gene as the marker gene for that sample. Additionally, for TNBC cases, in which the cell of origin tends to be basal, we used ACTA2 as the basal layer marker. Supplementary Table S11 contains correlation values for this analysis. 2D Manual Gene Discovery We also used manual annotation for Visium sections, in which resolution of expression is limited and not amenable to the techniques used in 2D automated gene discovery. For this, we implemented a manual workflow where a minimum of five areas each of normal, DCIS, and IDC in breast—or normal, HGPIN, and GP3+ in prostate—morphology were randomly manually annotated. Mean feature expression was then calculated for each area, and the Student t test was used to quantify differences between different morphologies. Annotated barcodes (Supplementary Table S12) and comparison statistics (Supplementary Table S11) can be found in the supplement. 3D Gene Discovery We further strengthened our gene discovery approach with multiplatform, 3D serial section DEG discovery. With this approach, we were able to quantify gene expression changes throughout a single region as it transitioned from noninvasive to invasive morphology. For this we use two methods, morphology group–based and path-based comparisons. For both approaches, we used regions annotated as described in “Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions”. Expression and correlation values can be found in supplementary Tables S13 and S14, respectively. For morphology group–based discovery, regions were annotated for morphology (DCIS, MI, or IDC in breast; normal, HGPIN, or GP3 in prostate), and mean gene expression was calculated for each region. We then, on a data type–specific basis, used the Student t test and fold change to quantify differences between morphology groups where possible. Due to variation in rate and location of region transition, the same spatial platform did not always capture each morphologic state for every interconnected region. Fold change was calculated as [( b + 1) − ( a + 1)]/( a + 1), in which a and b are arrays of expression values associated with different morphology groups. For path-based discovery, we calculated a single correlation value across multiple spatial platforms for each interconnected region. First, expression values for each data type were z-scaled within each data type. We then ran a linear regression on the scaled expression values for each Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD cross-section in the transitioning region. Values were ordered from least invasive end of the interconnect region to the most invasive. As such, positive correlations indicate increased expression toward the invasive end of the region, whereas negative values indicate the opposite, with increased expression in less-invasive areas of the region. 3D TAM Proximity Analysis For the six Xenium sections from sample HT704B1, we performed a 3D proximity analysis to evaluate the spatial relationship between macrophages and epithelial regions. First, TAMs were subtyped into two populations: SPP1 + TAMs and MS4A6A + TAMs. Cell annotation was based on transcript detection using the following criteria. A cell was classified as an SPP1 + TAM if it contained at least one transcript of any macrophage marker ( CD68 , CD163 , CSF1R , or CD14 ), at least one transcript of SPP1 , and zero EPCAM transcripts. Similarly, a cell was classified as an MS4A6A + TAM if it contained at least one transcript of any macrophage marker ( CD68 , CD163 , CSF1R , or CD14 ), at least one transcript of MS4A6A , and zero EPCAM transcripts. Next, we computed the shortest 3D distance from each TAM to the nearest epithelial region using spatial coordinates across all sections. For each epithelial region, we calculated a basal-layer intensity score, defined as the z-scored transcript counts of basal-layer boundary markers described in the “2D Automated Gene Discovery” “Methods” section. Higher basal-layer intensity scores correspond to regions with stronger basal integrity, consistent with less invasive DCIS morphology, whereas lower scores indicate reduced basal integrity characteristic of more invasive IDC regions. This approach assigns each TAM the basal-layer intensity score of its nearest epithelial region, providing a quantitative measure of the invasiveness of the epithelial environment in which each TAM resides. IF Validation Immunostaining was performed as described ( 100 ). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm thickness and placed on Superfrost Plus slides and baked at 60°C overnight before deparaffinization. The next day, tissues were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated in ethanol, and washed in ddH2O before heat-induced antigen retrieval with 0.1 mmol/L Tris-EDTA buffer pH9 (#NB900-62085, Novus) for 10 minutes using a steamer. These slides were incubated with 100 mmol/L glycine for 2 × 10 minutes and a blocking solution (5% inactivated normal donkey serum and 10 mg/mL BSA) for 1 hour at room temperature. Subsequently slides were incubated with primary antibodies in a humidified chamber overnight at 4°C. After washing with PBST 3 × 5 minutes, samples were incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature and washed with PBST 4 × 5 minutes. After incubation with Hoechst for 5 minutes, the slides were washed again in PBST for 5 minutes and mounted with VectaMount AQ Aqueous Mounting Medium (#H-5501-60; Southern Biotech). Primary antibodies used were from Abcam: rabbit monoclonal anti-ANPEP (AB_10866195;1:100), rabbit polyclonal anti-ALDH1A3 (AB_2937054;1:100), rabbit polyclonal anti-FASN (AB_732316,1:100), and rabbit monoclonal anti-GDF15 (AB_3099455, 1:100); LSBio: rabbit polyclonal anti-EPHA6 (AB_3741541; 1:100); Life Technologies: mouse monoclonal anti-PanCK (AB_10942225;1:200) and anti-CK5 (AB_2538529, 1:200) antibodies and Alexa Fluor 488-, 594-, and 647-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000); and R&D Biosytems: goat polyclonal anti–E-cadherin (AB_355568;1:100). The fluorescence images were obtained using Keyence Fluorescence Microscope (BZ-X810; Keyence). Normal, precancer, and cancer regions were annotated using Napari, and average intensities were calculated within each region. Breast and Prostate Cancer Proliferation and Migration Assays Human breast and prostate cancer cell lines ETCC-006 ( CVCL_6G19 ), ETCC-010 ( CVCL_6G22 ), and PC3 ( CVCL_E2RM ) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) in (March, 2022). Cell line profiling was not performed by the authors following receipt from the ATCC. Cells were used for experiments within 10 passages after thawing and were not maintained in culture for longer than 2 months. Cells were routinely tested for Mycoplasma contamination using the MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Lonza, #LT07-318), and the most recent test was performed in (August, 2025), with negative results. Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, #11875093) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, #16140071) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, #15140122) and maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . For prostate cancer experiments, we initially screened four commonly used prostate cancer cell lines for expression of the candidate genes ( GDF15 , FASN , ALDH1A3 , and ANPEP ). Among these, only PC3 cells expressed all four genes and were therefore selected for subsequent functional assays (Supplementary Fig. S11). To knock down the expression of the target gene ( MGP and PLAT in breast cancer cells and GDF15 , ANPEP , ALDH1A3 , and FASN in prostate cancer cell), lentiviral particles encoding specific shRNA as well as control shRNA were purchased from Sigma using the pLKO.1 vector. Cells were seeded in six-well plates and transduced with lentivirus in the presence of 10 μg/mL polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich, #TR-1003-G). After 48 hours, cells were selected using 10 μg/mL puromycin (Sigma-Aldrich, #P8833) for 7 days to establish stable knockdown cell lines. Cells surviving puromycin selection were expanded and used for downstream experiments within five passages. Knockdown efficiency was confirmed by RT-qPCR. The shRNA sequence for MGP and PLAT was GCGGTAGTAACTTTGTGTTAT and CAAGGTTTACACAGCACAGAA, respectively. GDF15, FASN, ALDH1A3, and ANPEP shRNA target sequence was CCGGATACTCACGCCAGAAGT, CATGGAGCGTATCTGTGAGAA, GCTGTATTAGAACCCTCAGAT, and ACCAGTACAGCGAGGTTAATG, respectively. Total RNA from cell lines was extracted using RNA extraction Kit (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. One microgram of total RNA was reverse transcribed using a cDNA synthesis kit (Themo Fisher Scientific, High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit with RNase Inhibitor, #4374966). qPCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (BIO-RAD, iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix, #1725121) on a QuantStudio or ABI 7500 system. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method, with ACTB and GAPDH as the internal control. The primer sequence for MGP was TCCGAGAACGCTCTAAGCCT; GCAAAGTCTGTAGTCATCACAGG. The primer sequence for PLAT was AGCGAGCCAAGGTGTTTCAA; CTTCCCAGCAAATCCTTCGGG. The primer sequence for ACTB was CATGTACGTTGCTATCCAGGC; CTCCTTAATGTCACGCACGAT. The primer for GAPDH was purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (Ref #580480971; 580480972). The primer sequence for FASN was TTCTACGGCTCCACGCTCTTCC; GAAGAGTCTTCGTCAGCCAGGA, and that for GDF15 was GTTAGCCAAAGACTGCCACTG; CCTTGAGCCCATTCCACA. The primer sequence for ALDH1A3 was TGGATCAACTGCTACAACGC; CACTTCTGTGTATTCGGCCA. The primer sequence for ANPEP was GACCAAAGTAAAGCGTGGAATCG; TCTCAGCGTCACCCGGTAG. Cell proliferation was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo). Cells (2,000–4,000 per well) were seeded in 96-well plates in triplicate. At indicated time points (e.g., 0, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 120 hours), 10 μL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader (BioTek or Thermo). Normal control, MGP -KD (knockdown), PLAT -KD, GDF15 -KD, FASN -KD, ALDH1A3 -KD, and ANPEP -KD cells were seeded in six-well plates and grown to about 100% confluence. A straight scratch was made using a sterile 200-μL pipette tip across the cell monolayer. Detached cells were removed by washing with PBS, and fresh serum-free medium was supplemented. Images were captured at 0 hours and after 24 hours using a light microscope (×5 magnification). The wound area was measured using ImageJ software, and migration was quantified as the percentage of wound closure. evidence_text:
Human adult and pediatric multimodal transcriptomic atlas of progression from pressure-loaded to failing right ventricle. Right ventricular failure (RVF) independently predicts mortality in heart failure, yet its pathophysiology is poorly understood. Here we present a multi-modal atlas of human right ventricular pressure loading and failure, including bulk (n = 142), single-nucleus (n = 11) and Xenium spatial (n = 9) transcriptomics in adults, plus pediatric (n = 14) and mouse pulmonary artery banding cohorts. Subclustering resolved 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages along a two-phase trajectory. Phase 1 (non-failing to pressure-loaded) accounts for most of the transcriptional change detectable by bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing and is marked by loss of resident macrophage identity, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and erosion of tissue-protective programs. Phase 2 (pressure-loaded to RVF) produces little change in bulk RNA sequencing but is resolved by spatial transcriptomics, engaging multi-lineage fibrotic, endothelial-activation and cardiomyocyte-reactivation programs, with a gain of extracellular matrix (collagen, laminin, thrombospondin) signaling over a stable cell contact adhesion baseline. Mitochondrial respirometry revealed respiratory dysfunction in adult and mouse RVF but not pediatric RVF. Multi-lineage remodeling of the cardiac microenvironment emerges as the central molecular program of RVF, meriting further study as possible disease-modifying targets. Main  The normal right ventricle (RV) is morphologically and embryologically unique from the left ventricle (LV), precluding the categorical extrapolation of our understanding of left-side pathophysiology to the right heart  1  . Historically, cardiac research has focused on left ventricular failure (LVF), delivering multiple approved therapies, with less attention to RVF  2  . Although the most common cause of RVF is pressure overload secondary to LVF, RVF can also arise from diverse other causes  3 – 5  . Independent of etiology, RV dysfunction portends a poor prognosis: patients with LVF and concomitant RV dysfunction have approximately a two-fold increased mortality risk  6 – 8  .  Advances in LVF therapy have been driven by targeting critical pathways such as the renin−angiotensin−aldosterone system (RAAS)  9  . Attempts to generalize these therapies to the RV have been clinically unsuccessful. Neurohormonal blockade, a cornerstone of LVF therapy, has little efficacy in RVF  9  . There is, therefore, a need for exploratory research to identify RVF-specific therapeutic targets.  We conducted a multi-platform transcriptomic study of failing and non-failing human RVs, integrating bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (142 individuals), single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) (11 individuals) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics (nine sections), with mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histological validation. We placed these findings in broader context by comparing to a mouse pulmonary artery banding (PAB) model, pediatric single-ventricle RVs, LVF and a published pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) RV transcriptomic dataset. Recent human cardiac snRNA-seq atlases remain LV centric  10 – 14   or include limited RV in genetically defined cohorts  15  . Although some include non-failing (NF) RV tissue  11 , 14 , 16  , none has stratified pressure-overload RVF progression or integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial modalities on matched patient tissue. Here we present, to our knowledge, the first such integrated atlas and propose a two-phase model in which multi-lineage erosion of protective programs occurs in various cell types during the transition from NF to preserved RV in the context of LVF (NF → pRV) and is followed by a pRV → RVF transition that is comparatively muted in bulk RNA expression changes but engages a broader multi-lineage signal elicited in Xenium spatial pseudobulk analyses.    Results   Cohort and multi-platform approach  From the Penn Human Heart Tissue Bank, we collected transmural RV samples from adult NF organ donors and LVF transplant recipients, the latter substratified  17 , 18   into pressure-loaded but preserved systolic function (pRV) and failing (RVF) groups (Fig.  1a  and Supplementary Tables  1 – 3 ). We applied bulk RNA-seq ( n  = 142), snRNA-seq ( n  = 11; 61,398 nuclei) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( n  = 9 sections; 625,305 cells; 477-gene panel); a mouse PAB model at 2-week and 2-month timepoints; a pediatric snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 14; 10 hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)-palliated RVs stratified by normal function or RVF and four controls); and a cross-etiology comparison with a published PAH RVF bulk dataset  19  . Source data                      Bulk RNA-seq reveals the transcriptomic landscape of RV failure progression  Principal component analysis (PCA) of bulk RNA-seq separated NF from pRV/RVF but poorly separated pRV from RVF (Fig.  1b ). Differential expression (DE) yielded many NF versus pRV/RVF differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with strong NF → pRV and NF → RVF fold change (FC) correlation (Extended Data Fig.  1a,b  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Prominent DEGs common to pRV and RVF included cardiac stress ( NPPA ,  NPPB ), chemokines ( CXCL8 – 11 ) and extracellular matrix (ECM)/angiogenic genes. Pathway enrichment highlighted immune, complement and inflammatory terms (Supplementary Data  2 ), suggesting that immune populations dominate the bulk signal. Many DEGs exhibited stepwise changes from NF → pRV → RVF, with 115 stepwise-increasing genes enriched for T cell chemotaxis, and 161 stepwise-decreasing genes enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal components (Extended Data Fig.  1c–f  and Supplementary Data  3 ). Fewer significant DEGs were identified from pRV → RVF analysis, indicating that most transcriptional remodeling precedes functional decompensation. pRV-upregulated genes enriched for oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS); RVF-upregulated genes were immune dominated (Extended Data Fig.  1g,h  and Supplementary Data  2 ).                    We also evaluated DE by weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA)  20   to capture broader co-expression signals, resolving 29 gene modules, almost all of which were differentially expressed across states (Fig.  1c–e  and Supplementary Data  4 ). Two OXPHOS modules (M25 and M26) declined monotonically across NF → pRV → RVF at the module eigengene level, whereas the large resident macrophage module M1 ( CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  VSIG4 ) was highest in NF and fell sharply from NF to pRV before plateauing. In the opposing direction, an adaptive immune module (M8; T/B cell and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II) genes) rose significantly from NF to pRV (Fig.  1d,e  and Supplementary Data  4 ).  To test cross-etiology generalizability, we compared our bulk data to a published PAH-associated RVF transcriptome  19  . RVF versus NF yielded 235 concordantly downregulated genes (respiratory electron transport (ETC), complex I biogenesis) and 214 concordantly upregulated genes (interferon (IFN) α/β, antiviral signaling), establishing mitochondrial decline and IFN activation as etiology shared (Fig.  1f ). By contrast, the complement cascade was divergent between cohorts, downregulated in our RVF but upregulated in PAH RVF, identifying complement activation as an etiology-specific response (Extended Data Fig.  1i  and Supplementary Data  5 ).    Single-nucleus transcriptomics resolves 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages  Single-nucleus RNA-seq of 11 RV samples (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ) yielded 61,398 nuclei (2,912 genes per nucleus) and 12 major clusters (Fig.  2a,b  and Supplementary Data  6 ). Composition shifted progressively with disease: loss of cardiomyocyte nuclei and expansion of endothelial cell (EC) nuclei from NF → pRV → RVF (Fig.  2c ). This compositional shift parallels reports from LVF snRNA-seq atlases, although, notably, the non-myocyte expansion here is endothelial predominant without the fibroblast expansion typical of LVF  12  . Bulk WGCNA modules were assigned to dominant lineages (Fig.  2d ). Single-nucleus RNA-seq subclustering resolved 34 subtypes across 12 lineages: 10 cardiomyocyte, seven fibroblast, five EC, six myeloid and six lineages retained at lineage level (pericyte, smooth muscle, adipocyte, epicardial, neuronal/glial and natural killer/T) due to low counts (markers in Figs.  6b  and  7b , Extended Data Figs.  2b  and  3b  and Supplementary Data  7 ). Pseudobulk DESeq2 within each subtype across three pairwise comparisons (Supplementary Data  8  and  9 ) identified fibroblasts as most transcriptionally responsive (1,083 DEGs pRV versus NF; 806 DEGs RVF versus NF), followed by cardiomyocytes (248; 464). This difference partially reflects lower inter-patient dispersion among fibroblasts.                      Spatial transcriptomics extends and validates single-nucleus findings  We profiled nine transmural RV sections (one per patient; 625,305 cells; Supplementary Table  6 ) on 10x Xenium (477-gene panel; Supplementary Data  10 ). Annotation against the snRNA-seq reference produced concordant cell type assignments (Fig.  3a,b ). Pseudobulk DESeq2 (Supplementary Data  11 ) broadly corroborated snRNA-seq at the cross-platform FC level (Fig.  3c ), with spatial maps confirming consistent assignment across all sections (Fig.  3d ). There is also downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  (ref.   26  ) across all seven fibroblast subtypes and fibroblast activation ( SFRP4  (ref.   27  ),  THBS4  (ref.   28  )). Phase 2 is focal and cell type specific, not platform driven  Phase 2 lineage-level significant genes are 39 in Xenium, 61 in snRNA-seq and five in bulk (unique gene symbols per contrast), concordant in direction across platforms where detectable (Fig.  4b ). The signal concentrates in two lineages. In cardiomyocytes, Xenium reveals a BMP/TGFβ superfamily signaling program ( BMPR2 ,  BMPR1A, FSTL3 ,  BAMBI  up). This simultaneous upregulation of receptors and their inhibitors is cardiomyocyte restricted and opposite to the receptor loss of function of heritable PAH. In ECs, phase 2 resolves as an EndoMT/angiogenic destabilization program ( SNAI1 ,  ADAMTS1 ,  ANGPT2  up; directionally concordant in snRNA-seq). CCR2 −  macrophage remodeling remains graded rather than a discrete phase 2 step. Module-level analysis (Fig.  4c ) resolves two cross-platform concordant programs. A cardiomyocyte OXPHOS module set (M10, M25, M26) is progressively downregulated, whereas myeloid inflammatory, cytokine and immunoglobulin modules (M8, M13, M15) are coordinately induced. Spatially constrained cell−cell communication reveals stage-specific signaling  Cell−cell communication inference (CellChat  29  , applied to per-patient snRNA-imputed Xenium expression under Xenium-derived spatial constraints; Supplementary Data  14 ) revealed a progressive reorganization of myocardial signaling across the NF → pRV → RVF axis (Fig.  4e,f ). In every condition, the highest-probability pathways were contact-mediated adhesion programs (PTPRM, NCAM, ADGRL, CDH), consistent with the dense cellular packing of myocardium and serving as a stable baseline rather than a disease feature. Layered on this baseline, RVF showed a selective gain of ECM signaling: COLLAGEN, LAMININ and THBS, which were low or absent among top-ranked interactions in NF and pRV, rose to prominence specifically in RVF. This matrix signaling gain is concordant with the emergence of the matrifibrocyte-like fibroblast state and frames fibroblast-to-stroma communication as a defining feature of RVF. Fibroblasts activate early in RV failure  Fibroblasts were the most transcriptionally responsive snRNA-seq population (1,083 pRV versus NF DEGs; 806 RVF versus NF DEGs). Subclustering snRNA-seq resolved seven literature-grounded subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  3a,b ): Fb Resident, Adventitial, Elastogenic, Interstitial, Stressed, Pro-fibrotic and Anti-fibrotic, with fibroblast subtype proportions generally stable across disease states (Extended Data Fig.  3c ). The snRNA-seq trajectory was front loaded and consistent with Xenium (Extended Data Fig.  3d ): in phase 1, there was downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  along with  GPX3  and the matrix/elastogenic genes  ELN  and  TIMP3 . Simultaneously, the canonical myofibroblast/matricellular markers  THBS4  (ref.   34  ) and  ACTA2  (ref.   35  ) and the activated fibroblast marker  SFRP4  were induced.  None of the snRNA-seq, bulk or panel-filtered Xenium data yielded significant fibrogenic DEGs in RVF versus pRV at the lineage level. Xenium fibroblast subtype resolution exposed a focal phase 2 program restricted to activated/matricellular subsets involving  THBS4 ,  TNC  and  PRG4  (snRNA-seq directions concordant, not significant) (Extended Data Fig.  3e ). Two literature-defined module scores anchored the two-phase split: the Koenig et al.  10   donor fibroblast identity signature collapsed sharply at NF → pRV with no further drop at decompensation (Extended Data Fig.  3f ), whereas the Fu et al.  34   matrifibrocyte commitment signature was flat at NF → pRV and trended upward only at pRV → RVF (Extended Data Fig.  3g ). This suggests that fibroblast identity erosion is phase 1 specific, whereas fibrogenic commitment is phase 2 specific. Cross-platform similarity (Extended Data Fig.  3h,i ) was strongest for Stressed and Interstitial subtypes. Spatial neighborhood analysis (Extended Data Fig.  3j–l ) placed FB Stressed, Matrix, Intermediate and CILP in myeloid-enriched niches (Xen FB Matrix–myeloid Pearsonʼs  r  = 0.93). Massonʼs trichrome/Sirius Red histology confirmed progressive fibrosis (+5.9% area per stage; Extended Data Fig.  3m ). In RVF, the fibrotic myocardium niche occupies a smaller fraction of section area (Fig.  3g ). This does not necessarily represent less fibrosis, as niche proportions are compositional. They describe how section area is partitioned between neighborhoods, not how much matrix each neighborhood contains. The rising histologic collagen burden (Extended Data Fig.  3m ), the pRV → RVF gain of ECM signaling (Fig.  4e ) and the matrifibrocyte commitment trend (Extended Data Fig.  3g ) all measure matrix content or fibroblast state and are compatible with fibrotic remodeling intensifying within existing neighborhoods while the stressed myocardium and vascular niches expand their share of the section. Fibroblast subclusters identified from previous LV studies were similarly recovered (Extended Data Fig.  4a–d ), indicating conserved fibroblast biology across ventricles. Myeloid WGCNA (Fig.  6d–f ) recapitulated this pattern: RVF-upregulated M8 enriched for MHC-II master  CIITA   40  , whereas the RVF-downregulated  NR3C1  target-enriched M1 module captured the same coordinated resident identity loss. After co-embedding RV and LV (from Koenig et al.  10  ) myeloid cells (Extended Data Fig.  4e,f ), the same resident/scavenger markers,  VSIG4  and  CD163 , fell in both ventricles (Extended Data Fig.  4g,h ), identifying erosion of resident macrophage identity as a shared, chamber-independent feature of heart failure.  Within the myeloid compartment, the dominant transcriptional change was a coordinated, pan-myeloid downregulation of GR transactivation targets. The canonical GR transactivation targets  FKBP5 ,  TSC22D3 ,  ZBTB16  and  KLF9 — together with  ANGPTL4 —were concordantly downregulated as an early stepwise shift  23  , established at the pre-failure (pRV) stage and sustained in RVF (Fig.  6g,h  and Supplementary Data  17 ), and this decline was consistent across myeloid subtypes rather than confined to a single population. In parallel, MHC-II/antigen presentation genes, led by the master regulator  CIITA , were induced with the same early kinetics. Critically, this rewiring was program specific rather than a generalized inflammatory activation, and two innate immune axes that commonly accompany myocardial stress were explicitly unchanged across disease stage. The NLRP3 inflammasome, a canonical driver of heart failure inflammation, showed minimal induction of its sensors, adaptor, caspases or effector cytokines ( IL1B ,  IL18 )  41 , 42  . Likewise, the type I IFN/antiviral ISG response, increasingly reported in failing and inflamed myocardium, remained flat, arguing against an IFN-driven component to the myeloid response  43 , 44  . Thus, the failing RV myeloid compartment shows a focused, coordinated shift in GR target gene expression, in the absence of inflammasome or type I IFN activation. Comparison with failing LV (dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)) myeloid cells shows that this configuration is only partly conserved across ventricles: MHC-II/antigen presentation induction is shared, and the type I IFN response stays low in both, whereas the loss of GR target gene expression and the absence of inflammasome activation are RV specific. LV DCM myeloid cells instead retain GR target expression and show inflammasome induction (Extended Data Fig.  4i ).  Spatial Xenium refined myeloid taxonomy into eight subpopulations, adding Mac C1q and Mast Cell. Residents distributed broadly, and iMacs co-localized with monocytes at the tissue periphery—a spatial pattern that cannot by itself distinguish phenotypic transition of resident macrophages from monocyte-derived recruitment (Fig.  6i ). TLF marker retention in iMacs, iMac non-expansion (not significant by Kruskal−Wallis) and CCR2 −  contraction are consistent with phenotypic transition, but the iMac/monocyte spatial co-occurrence and absence of imaging-based lineage tracing leave the relative contribution of resident cell transition versus monocyte recruitment unresolved.
