Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. Our model-specific architecture comprises of three layers: two ECC (Edge-Conditioned Convolution) [ 50 ,  51 ] GCN layers [ 52 ,  53 ] followed by a ReLU activation function [ 54 ], and one linear transformation layer. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. To optimize computing efficiency, we initially conducted tests with 10% scaled-down images to obtain approximate scale and angle adjustments. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. evidence_text:
Protocol for integrated multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium and MACSima. Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  Multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on a single tissue section    •  Detailed Xenium and MACSima workflow protocol for single-section spatial multi-omics    •  Registration and integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data at single-cell level      Publisher’s note: Undertaking any experimental protocol requires adherence to local institutional guidelines for laboratory safety and ethics.    Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Dec 18.       Before you begin   Protocol overview  This protocol describes multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on the same tissue section using Xenium (10x Genomics) and MACSima Imaging Cyclic Staining (MICS, Miltenyi Biotec). The workflow was established using human tonsil and tumor tissue sections; however, it can be adapted to other tissue types with appropriate optimization of RNA probe panels, antibody panels, and tissue processing conditions.    Innovation  This protocol introduces a novel workflow for multimodal spatial profiling by integrating Xenium spatial transcriptomics with highly multiplexed protein imaging using MICS on the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarray (TMA) section. Alternative multimodal workflows have demonstrated the combination of Xenium with other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, including PhenoCycler and COMET.  1   ,   2   Building upon these advances, this protocol provides the first detailed experimental and computational workflow for integrating Xenium with the current-generation MACSima platform, which supports significantly higher antibody plexity than comparable technologies. This workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima analysis includes optimized requirements and procedures for sample processing, antigen retrieval, and iterative cyclic immunofluorescence that preserve tissue integrity and enable single-cell RNA and protein measurements on the same section. In addition to the experimental workflow, this protocol provides scripts for accurate registration of Xenium and MACSima imaging data, enabling direct correlation of transcriptomic and proteomic features within the same spatial framework. Importantly, both the laboratory workflow and computational approach can be adapted to other spatial multi-omics combinations, offering a flexible framework for integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data. Together, these advances address key technical challenges in spatial multi-omics and provide a reproducible and scalable approach for multimodal tissue analysis.    Institutional permissions  Experiments involving human-derived tissues require approval from the appropriate institutional ethics committee. Researchers must ensure that ethical approval is obtained and that informed consent is secured from all donors prior to sample collection. All specimens used in this study (see  key resources table ) were obtained with informed consent and handled in accordance with institutional regulations and approved protocols.    Tissue selection and preparation 
   1.  Obtain FFPE TMA samples with preserved morphology and RNA integrity.   
          CRITICAL:  Following proper handling, storage, preparation and sectioning of the FFPE tissues according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ) is critical to ensure preservation of morphology and RNA integrity.  
   2.  Optimize sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time for the block and floating time of the sections in the water bath of the Section Transfer System (STS) before mounting on slides to prevent cutting artefacts.    3.  Assess tissue quality, morphology and RNA integrity of the blocks prior to mounting on Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.    4.  Place sections on Xenium slides and store them according to standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).   a.  If the tissue blocks are of optimal quality, section them at 4–6 μm thickness using a microtome and mount the sections on Xenium slides.    b.  Dry the slides appropriately as per standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).      
          Pause point:  Slides can be stored at room temperature (RT, 20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in tubes with desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and Xenium workflow.  
   Xenium assay version compatibility 
    Note:   The workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima is compatible with the v1 as well as the 5K Prime Xenium assay versions. It is also compatible with the Xenium In situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation which has now become standard in the Xenium workflows. Since the MACSima workflow uses directly conjugated antibodies, the antibodies in the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit do not pose a risk of cross-detection (10x Genomics,  CG000750 ).  
   Xenium probe panel design 
   5.  Select a pre-designed Xenium probe panel and/or design a custom Xenium probe panel (to be used as a standalone panel or as an add-on to the pre-designed panel) targeting genes of interest relevant to the biological question.    6.  Validate the custom probe panel performance in control samples, if available.   
    Note:   Perform add-on panel design in line with the guidelines provided in the  Technical Note: Xenium Add-on Panel Design  (10x Genomics,  CG000643 ). Transcript abundance and cell type specificity should be taken into consideration when designing a panel.  
    Note:   Reference to existing single-cell RNA-seq data, ideally from matched sample types, can guide panel design by enabling identification of cell type specific genes and transcript abundance.  
    Note:   The custom probe panel performance can be cross-validated post-Xenium run by comparing with existing single-cell RNA-seq and / or Xenium datasets for sensitivity in terms of number of transcripts detected and for specificity in terms of biologically relevant co-expression patterns of different genes.  3    
   Antibody panel design for MACSima 
   7.  Select antibodies targeting proteins of interest for multiplex imaging and check for compatibility of antibodies with the respective sample type (FFPE).    8.  Optimize antibody concentrations and staining conditions in a mock Xenium-MACSima experiment using control samples, if available, to test the compatibility of sequential Xenium and MACSima staining (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).   
          CRITICAL:  Antibodies must be tested for compatibility within the Xenium-MACSima workflow (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).  
          CRITICAL:  Ensure that tissue processing conditions, such as working in an RNase-free environment, sectioning thickness, and optimal slide recovery and antigen retrieval conditions post-Xenium are compatible with both Xenium RNA detection and downstream protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Check for tissue integrity after post-Xenium imaging slide recovery (steps 12 and 13 in the  step-by-step method details ) before continuing with the protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Optimize post-Xenium antigen retrieval conditions to achieve sufficient epitope accessibility for protein staining while preserving tissue integrity. Harsh antigen retrieval conditions can compromise tissue integrity and spatial registration between modalities.

The following upstream processing steps are performed once per slide before the per-core registration loop and are summarized here for context. The code for these steps is experiment-specific and is not included in the shared repository; however, the analysis workflow follows standard practices using scanpy  7   and the Segment Anything Model (SAM).  8      12.  Build AnnData  9   feature matrix.   a.  Load each Xenium output folder by reading the transcript table (transcripts.parquet).    b.  Filter for quality value (QV) ≥ 20, remove control probes, and aggregate transcript counts per nucleus using nucleus boundary polygons (nucleus_boundaries.parquet).    c.  Store the resulting count matrix, centroid coordinates, and nucleus areas as an AnnData object.       13.  Segment TMA cores.   a.  Identify individual TMA cores using the Segment Anything Model (SAM1, ViT-H) applied to a 2D cell density histogram (binned centroids at approximately 50 μm per pixel). Each detected mask corresponds to one TMA core.    b.  Assign a position label to each cell according to which mask their centroid falls within and flag cells outside all masks with is_in_core = False.       14.  Perform quality filtering.   a.  Remove cells that are not assigned to a core and filter the remaining cells according to transcript counts and/or size.          Note:   A commonly used approach for cell-level quality filtering is to exclude cells with fewer than ten transcripts and genes expressed in less than five cells ( https://squidpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/tutorials/tutorial_xenium.html ).  10   However, transcript counts per cell are dependent both on the tissue and gene panel  11   and thus the use of more or less stringent thresholds taking into account also the area of the cell might be required.  12   Finally, a visual inspection of the spatial distribution of the excluded cells can help to identify biases in the filtering by highlighting the presence of spatially organized clusters of excluded cells.  11       15.  Match the TMA cores between Xenium and MACSima data.   a.  Match the Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers manually by comparing a spatial scatter plot of Xenium cell positions (colored by core position) with the MACSima ROI overview image.    b.  Write this mapping as a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.         Planning of multimodal data integration  This protocol describes the cross-modal alignment of Xenium spatial transcriptomics data (10x Genomics) with MACSima multiplexed cyclic immunofluorescence imaging data (Miltenyi Biotec) for TMA samples. Integration is performed per TMA core and produces multi-modal SpatialData  13   objects saved as Zarr  14   archives.     Step-by-step method details 
    Note:   The protocol was optimized for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with Cell Segmentation Staining, using a Prime 5K Human pan Tissue and Pathways panel (10x Genomics, PN-1000724) and a custom 100-gene add-on panel. For alternative Xenium workflow formats, workflow parameters may require adaptation. Xenium processing should always be performed according to the corresponding manufacturer-recommended protocols. In addition, performance of downstream antibody staining following Xenium processing may vary depending on the selected Xenium assay configuration.  
  Preparation of FFPE TMA sections 
          Timing: 3 days when performing steps consecutively. Approximately 1.5 days are required for sectioning optimization, slide mounting, drying, and quality assessment. Another day is required for sectioning, mounting to Xenium slides, and drying. Half a day is required for deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of sections.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA samples for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow, including sectioning of the FFPE blocks, tissue mounting, deparaffinization, and decrosslinking of sections. Sample preparation is performed according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).           CRITICAL:  Sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time of the FFPE TMA block in ice-cold water, should be optimized depending on tissue type, degree of dehydration, and the age of the paraffin block. Similarly, the floating time of sections in the water bath prior to mounting on Xenium slides needs to be adjusted to prevent wrinkling, folding, or tearing of the sections.     1.  Assess tissue quality and RNA integrity.    Note:   Evaluate tissue quality and RNA integrity of the FFPE TMA samples prior to placement of sections onto Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.     a.  Mount serial sections on SuperFrost Plus slides and deparaffinize according to the standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).    b.  Perform DAPI and H&E staining as outlined in the demonstrated protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Appendix).    c.  Image the slide to assess nuclear integrity, tissue morphology, sectioning artefacts, and the presence of necrotic or degraded regions.    d.  For RNA quality assessment, collect approximately four 10 μm sections (for samples ≤ 6.5 × 6.5 mm) for RNA extraction and DV200 analysis.          CRITICAL:  Samples with DV200 values below 30 % are considered suboptimal and may result in reduced median transcript counts per cell in downstream Xenium analysis.         2.  Section the FFPE TMA block and dry the sections.          CRITICAL:  During sectioning, maintain RNase-free conditions by wiping the microtome with RNase Zap ™ solution and filling the water bath of the STS with nuclease-free water.     a.  Prepare the FFPE TMA block for sectioning by rehydrating it in ice-cold Milli-Q water for a previously optimized duration (typically 10–30 min, depending on tissue type and degree of dehydration).    b.  Trim the block until the area of interest is fully exposed. For previously sectioned TMA blocks, discard the first 5–10 sections to obtain uniformly hydrated and intact tissue sections prior to collection.    c.  Section FFPE TMA block at a thickness of 5 μm using a microtome. Let the sections slide via the STS into its water bath filled with nuclease-free water and maintained at 42°C–45°C.    d.  Incubate the sections in the water bath for a previously optimized duration (typically 10 s to 3 min for most FFPE tissues) to allow the section to fully flatten and to minimize wrinkles, folds, or tearing prior to mounting.          CRITICAL:  Excessive incubation times in the water bath may lead to tissue distortion or reduced adherence during downstream processing.      e.  From the water bath, mount the sections carefully onto the Xenium slides (10× Genomics, PN-1000465), within the designated sample area.          CRITICAL:  Avoid placing the sections covering the fiducials, specifically the top and bottom fiducials.            CRITICAL:  Monitor the section adhesion on Xenium slides throughout the workflow to ensure that sections remain intact and properly attached during all processing steps.      f.  Following section placement, incubate the slides at 42°C for 3 h to promote adhesion of the sections to the Xenium slide surface.    g.  After incubation, place the slides in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing desiccant and store them overnight (16–24 h) at RT (20°C–25°C) to allow complete drying of the tissue sections.          Pause point:  Following section mounting, Xenium slides can be stored at RT (20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in the presence of desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and further processing with the Xenium workflow.         3.  Perform deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of the sections.   a.  Incubate the slides at 60°C for 2 h, followed by cooling at RT (20°C–25°C) for 7 min prior to further processing.    b.  Sequentially incubate the slides in two Coplin jars containing xylene for 10 min each.    c.  Perform two washes in 100 % ethanol for 3 min each.    d.  Perform two washes in 96 % ethanol for 3 min each.    e.  Perform one wash in 70 % ethanol for 3 min.    f.  Perform a final rinse in nuclease-free water for 20 s.    Note:   Xylene and ethanol incubation steps should be performed in a fume hood.      g.  Assemble the slides into Xenium cassettes.    h.  Perform decrosslinking using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000720) (included in the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  kit, 10x Genomics, PN-1000742).    i.  Immediately proceed with the Xenium in situ gene expression workflow.         Probe hybridization for Xenium Prime  in situ  gene expression 
          Timing: 2–3 days; with the Xenium  in situ  multimodal cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 3 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, and cell segmentation staining. Day 3 includes post-staining washes, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining. Without cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 2 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining.   
 This section describes the preparation of deparaffinized and decrosslinked FFPE TMA sections for the Xenium workflow, enabling subsequent imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer. The entire workflow is performed according to the  Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation  user guide (10x Genomics,  CG000760 ) using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  reagents (10× Genomics, PN-1000742).    4.  Perform priming and probe hybridization.   a.  Hybridize priming oligos to decrosslinked RNA.    b.  Perform RNase treatment and a polishing reaction to release the RNA strand from the hybridized oligos, thereby enabling subsequent hybridization of Xenium probes to the target RNA (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).    c.  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, C1000) using the Xenium Prime 5K probes ( Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay  kit, 10× Genomics, PN-1000671) together with an optional custom human add-on panel comprising up to 100 additional genes.       5.  Perform post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification.   a.  Perform post-hybridization washes to remove unbound probes, followed by ligation of hybridized probes, and enzymatic rolling circle amplification to generate amplified signal products for downstream imaging.       6.  Perform optional multimodal cell segmentation staining.   a.  To facilitate morphology-based cell segmentation, perform overnight (16–24 h) staining using the Xenium cell segmentation staining reagents, which label nuclei, cell boundaries, and intracellular RNA-rich regions according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).       7.  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclear staining.   a.  After amplification (and optional cell segmentation staining), perform autofluorescence quenching, brief drying at 37°C for 5 min and subsequent nuclear staining according to the manufacturer’s instructions.    b.  Upon completion of the workflow, store the slides in 0.05 % PBST until imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer.                Pause point:  After completion of the Xenium sample preparation workflow and prior to loading onto the Xenium Analyzer, slides can be stored in 0.05 % PBST at 4°C in the dark for up to 1 week using a new Xenium cassette lid.      Note:   During the drying step following autofluorescence quenching, inspect the slides to ensure that the Xenium slide fiducials, particularly the top and bottom fiducials, remain free of tissue coverage. If fiducials are obstructed, carefully remove the tissue from these regions at the end of sample preparation, as covered fiducials may interfere with subsequent imaging and alignment on the Xenium Analyzer.      Note:   At the end of sample preparation, clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 70 % ethanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.     Xenium  in situ  gene expression imaging 
          Timing: 2.5–5 days; half a day is needed for hands-on preparation, including buffer preparation and setup of the Xenium Analyzer. An additional 2–5 days are required for instrument run time, depending on the Xenium assay version (e.g., Xenium v.1, Xenium Prime 5K), whether cell segmentation staining is performed, and the size and number of ROIs.   
 This section describes the setup and operation of the Xenium Analyzer for imaging and preliminary analysis of FFPE TMA sections prepared using the Xenium workflow.           CRITICAL:  In cases where a custom panel (add-on or standalone) is used, obtain the corresponding JSON file for the panel and upload it to the Xenium Analyzer prior to initiating the run.            CRITICAL:  Slides processed using different Xenium workflows cannot be run simultaneously in the same instrument run. However, slides processed with different probe panels within the same workflow can be run together during a single instrument run.      Note:   For the Xenium Prime workflow, ensure that the Xenium Analyzer software version is XA v3.0 or higher.     8.  Prepare buffers and set up the Xenium Analyzer.   a.  Prepare all required buffers and decoding reagents and set up the Xenium Analyzer for processing of slides generated using the Xenium workflow according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ). Use the  Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents  (10× Genomics, PN-1000740),  Xenium Decoding Consumables v2  (10× Genomics, PN-1000726), and  Xenium Reagent Bottles  (10× Genomics, PN-1000730).          Note:   Transfer the  Xenium Prime Decoding Reagent Module B  (sealed in the mylar bag) from −20°C to 4°C at least one day before the run and allow it to thaw at 4°C for 16–72 h.  This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA sections for MICS after the Xenium run and includes quencher removal, antigen retrieval, DAPI pre-staining, and dust particle removal. Following Xenium imaging, perform quencher removal as recommended in  Xenium In Situ Gene Expression – Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining  (10x Genomics,  CG000613 ) to reduce residual Xenium-associated background signals and improve compatibility with downstream cyclic immunofluorescence imaging using MACSima.    12.  Remove the quencher (see  problem 1  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  In a fume hood, prepare quencher removal solution by weighing 17.4 mg sodium hydrosulfite and transfer it to a conical tube containing 10 mL Milli-Q water.    b.  Cap the tube tightly and vortex for 10 s until the reagent is fully dissolved.    c.  Keep the solution at RT (20°C–25°C) until use.          CRITICAL:  Prepare quencher removal solution immediately before each use to ensure optimal performance, as its effectiveness decreases after 10 min.      Note:   Because sodium hydrosulfite is hazardous, prepare the solution in a fume hood.      Note:   Vortexing may be performed outside the fume hood if the tube is tightly capped.      Note:   Do not use alternative chemicals for quencher removal.      d.  Add 10 mL quencher removal solution into the slide mailer.    e.  Prepare three slide mailers with 10 mL Milli-Q water each.    f.  Gently immerse Xenium slide into the slide mailer with quencher removal solution and incubate for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).    g.  Immerse slide in each Milli-Q water containing slide mailer for 1 min, then move to the next one.    h.  Transfer the Xenium slide into a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with MACSima Running buffer until further use.    Note:   Alternatively, transfer Xenium slide into a MACSwell One Small imaging frame ( Figure 1 A, right) and add 1.5 mL quencher removal solution. After 10 min incubation at RT (20°C–25°C), wash slide with 1.5 mL Milli-Q water three times, waiting for 1 min each time.      Note:   Residual purple staining after Xenium processing indicates the presence of autofluorescence quencher and should disappear following successful quencher removal ( Figure 1 B).         13.  Perform heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER).   a.  Prepare the 10× stock solution of TEC antigen retrieval buffer at pH 9.0.    Note:   The 10x stock solution can be stored at 4°C for up to 3 months.      b.  Immediately before use, dilute the 10x stock to 1x working solution.    c.  Adjust the pH to 9.0.    d.  Preheat the 1× working solution to 95°C in a pressure cooker.    e.  Place the Xenium slide in a slide mailer and immerse it in the preheated TEC buffer. Incubate for 20 min at 95°C.          CRITICAL:  Ensure the slide is fully submerged and does not touch the pressure cooker container.            CRITICAL:  Avoid using open-bottom slide mailers, as air bubbles could directly contact the tissue section and cause partial lifting or detachment from the slide surface.      Note:   Depending on the antibody panel, alternative antigen retrieval buffers may be required (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).      f.  After incubation, remove the pressure cooker container and transfer it to a pre-cooled water bath (ice-cold) for cooling.    g.  When the buffer has reached RT (20°C–25°C), carefully remove the slide from the buffer.    h.  Dry the edges with a lint-free wipe to remove excess liquid.    i.  Mount the slide onto a MACSwell One Small imaging frame.    Note:   The MACSwell One Small imaging frame accommodates the Xenium imaging area optimally and enables complete coverage of the imaged region ( Figure 1 A).      j.  Add 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer.       14.  Pre-stain the sample with DAPI and remove dust particles.   a.  Incubate the Xenium slide with DAPI staining solution at a 1:5 dilution using MACSima Running Buffer (final concentration 1 μg/mL) in the dark for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).          CRITICAL:  Protect the slide from light during DAPI incubation to prevent photobleaching.      Note:   Ensure the staining solution fully covers the section.      b.  Wash the slides three times with 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer to remove excess dye.    c.  Check the TMA section under bright transmitted light to ensure there are no dust particles or debris in the experimental area.    d.  Remove any visible dust or debris, as these can interfere with imaging quality.    e.  Cover the slide with a final experimental volume of 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer and seal with pierceable aluminum foil.    Note:   Clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 2-propanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.            Pause point:  Store slides in running buffer at 4°C for ≤1 week. Add reagent panels and/or individual antibodies to the procedure.    c.  Adjust staining and imaging parameters as needed, including dilution factor, incubation time, exposure settings, bleaching conditions, and wash parameters.    d.  Recalculate imaging cycles after all reagents and parameters have been defined or assign the antibodies to the individual cycles manually.    Note:   When manually assigning antibodies to imaging cycles, consider the following guidelines:     i.  Avoid placing multiple markers targeting the same cell type in the same cycle.    ii.  Preferably place low-abundance, transiently expressed, activation-dependent markers, cytokines, and chemokines in earlier cycles, as their detection can be more challenging.    iii.  Place abundant, constitutively expressed, or structural proteins in later cycles, as they provide more robust signals.    iv.  Evaluate receptors and ligands individually based on antigen abundance, subcellular localization, and expected staining performance.    v.  Avoid FITC for broadly expressed or critical phenotyping markers because of its relatively low photostability and potential signal loss during image acquisition.    vi.  For alternative fluorochromes (e.g., Alexa Fluor dyes), empirically determine the bleaching intensity required for efficient signal removal or perform at least two bleaching cycles before staining with the subsequent conjugated antibody in that channel.    vii.  Avoid combining strongly expressed FITC signals with weak PE signals in the same cycle to minimize spectral overlap and signal interference.      Note:   The cell-type annotations and obs_name_orig identifiers are generated during upstream processing (see  before you begin ). The obs_name_orig field links each cell to its original Xenium cell boundary polygon.     26.  Load Xenium core mappings.   a.  Load the H5AD file, filter to the target slide and position, and retain only cells flagged as is_in_core.       27.  Load Xenium Spatial Data.   a.  Load cell/nucleus boundaries, cell labels, transcripts, expression matrix, and the morphology focus images from the Xenium output folder.       28.  Perform the per-core Registration Loop ( Figures 6 C and 6D).   a.  For each position-ROI pair, execute Steps 29–37 below. Pairs where the output Zarr folder already exists are automatically skipped.       29.  Align Observation Tables.   a.  Join annotated metadata with the Xenium cell table by cell_id/obs_name_orig. Filter to the highlighted position and set obsm['spatial'] from centroid coordinates (cell_centroid_x, cell_centroid_y).       30.  Load the MACSima images.   a.  Load the DAPI channel for the first cycle as well as all other non-DAPI and non-background channels.       31.  Compute Core Bounding Box.   a.  Derive the ROI bounding box in pixel coordinates from the spatial extent of the aligned cell table.       32.  Transform Cell/Nucleus Boundary Polygons and crop the Xenium dataset.   a.  Scale each polygon by the transform_factor (micrometers to pixels).    b.  Translate it by subtracting the bounding box origin multiplied by scale_factor, placing the boundaries in the same coordinate space as the full-resolution images.       33.  Perform a Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)-Based Image Registration.  19     a.  Perform downscaling by scale_factor, using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().  20      b.  Apply Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE)  21   with skimage.exposure.equalize_adapthist()  22   with default parameters: clip_limit = 0.01, kernel_size = 1/8 of image dimensions.    c.  Convert pixel values to uint8.    Note:   The downscaling by scale_factor = 3 reduces runtime and suppresses high-frequency photon noise during feature detection. If registration fails or produces poor results, try scale_factor = 2 for higher-resolution feature detection or adjust CLAHE parameters.  21        d.  Detect SIFT key points and match descriptors with Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN)  23   (Parameters: KD-tree, 5 trees, 50 checks).    e.  Apply Lowe’s ratio test  19   with threshold 0.5 to retain high-confidence matches.    f.  Compute a 2D affine transformation from the surviving inlier matches using spatialdata.transformations.get_transformation_between_landmarks().    g. Expected outcomes  Successful implementation of this protocol results in the generation of a multimodal spatial dataset containing both transcriptomic and proteomic information from the same FFPE TMA section. The wet-lab workflow provides practical guidance for the critical experimental steps required for successful Xenium and MICS procedures, including tissue preparation, Xenium processing, post-Xenium slide recovery, antigen retrieval, antibody staining, and multiplexed imaging. Important considerations and troubleshooting insights are provided throughout to help users optimize tissue integrity, RNA and protein signal quality, and overall assay performance. Following Xenium spatial transcriptomics and subsequent MICS, users obtain high-resolution spatial maps of RNA transcripts and protein markers while preserving tissue morphology and spatial context. The experimental workflow enables detection of thousands of RNA targets using the Xenium platform together with highly multiplexed protein profiling using MICS. The workflow is expected to enable comprehensive multimodal characterization of individual cells by combining Xenium transcriptomic information with highly multiplexed and customizable protein profiling. The increased antibody plexity and flexibility of MACSima compared with the protein-detection capabilities of Xenium and other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, such as PhenoCycler and COMET, enable broader phenotypic and functional characterization, particularly in complex immune and tumor microenvironments. Following image registration and protein channel intensity quantification, transcriptomic and proteomic measurements are linked at single-cell resolution, generating a combined RNA-protein expression matrix for each cell together with its spatial coordinates within the tissue. The resulting dataset can be used to identify and characterize cellular phenotypes, investigate cell states, study cell-cell interactions, and explore tissue organization by integrating complementary transcriptomic and proteomic information. In addition, the image registration and data integration framework provided in this protocol can be adapted to combine Xenium data with other multiplex imaging modalities.  Users should expect preservation of tissue integrity throughout the workflow, successful recovery of Xenium-processed slides for downstream protein imaging, and generation of registered multimodal datasets suitable for downstream spatial and single-cell analyses. Depending on tissue quality, RNA integrity, antibody performance, and imaging conditions, signal intensity and the number of detected transcripts or proteins may vary between samples.  After step 35 (SpatialData assembly), the output Zarr store contains aligned images from both modalities, transformed cell and nucleus segmentation polygons ( Figure 7 D), the gene expression count matrix with cell-type annotations, and spatially filtered transcript coordinates. The data can be visualized interactively with napari using the napari-spatialdata plugin, where all layers overlay correctly in a shared coordinate space.  After step 36 (protein quantification,  Figure 6 D), each cell in registration.aligned_data[”rna_protein_table”].X contains numeric columns for each MACSima antibody. A cross-modal concordance between RNA-based cell-type annotations and protein measurements can serve as an additional quality metric for the overall registration and quantification workflow. This concordance could be visually explored by plotting heatmaps showing the expression of corresponding RNA and protein markers for each of the identified cells using standard tools such as scanpy.  7   The correlation coefficients between transcript counts and mean protein expression per cell for pairs of corresponding markers can also be used for a quantitative evaluation of the concordance between RNA and protein measurements.  2    After step 37 (registration quality assessment), the color overlay should show white overlap at nuclear positions, with minimal red-only or green-only fringes ( Figure 7 C).    Quantification and statistical analysis  The per-cell protein quantification (step 36,  Figure 6 D) yields absolute fluorescence intensity values (mean of aligned pixel values within each cell mask). These values are instrument- and acquisition-specific and should be used for within-experiment comparisons. Cross-experiment normalization (e.g., percentile normalization or z-score per channel) may be necessary when integrating multiple MACSima runs. It is important to note that errors in per-cell protein quantification could substantially affect downstream analysis. Per-cell protein quantification depends on accurate image registration and cell segmentation, as fluorescence intensity is calculated from the pixels within each cell mask. The sensitivity to segmentation errors may vary according to subcellular localization: nuclear markers are generally less affected by small changes in cell boundaries, whereas membrane-associated markers may be more sensitive to segmentation inaccuracies, particularly at cell-cell interfaces. Cytoplasmic markers typically show intermediate sensitivity. Applications requiring improved or alternative segmentation, advanced segmentation approaches can be evaluated and compared with the default segmentation approach to assess their suitability for the respective tissue and marker composition. Therefore, segmentation quality and image alignment should be carefully assessed before interpreting per-cell fluorescence intensities.  The combined RNA and protein measurements are stored in a single AnnData table within the SpatialData Zarr store. Downstream analyses, including joint RNA and protein cell-type classification, ligand-receptor interaction inference, and spatial neighborhood analysis, can be performed using standard tools (e.g., scanpy,  7   squidpy,  28   LIANA  29  ) applied to the exported AnnData table.    Limitations  Antibody performance may vary between tissue types. For example, we observed tissue-dependent variation in staining performance in the data generated in the scope of this workflow. Therefore, as described in  before you begin  (step 7) and in  problem 2  in  troubleshooting , antibody performance should be validated in the tissue type of interest e.g., by performing a mock Xenium-MACSima.  The SIFT-based registration relies on sufficient structural similarity between the Xenium DAPI morphology focus image and the MACSima DAPI staining. If tissue morphology is substantially altered between the two acquisitions (e.g., due to tissue loss, folding, or deformation during antigen retrieval), registration may fail or produce locally poor alignment. In such cases, non-rigid (deformable) registration methods may be required but are not implemented in this workflow (see  problem 6  in  troubleshooting ).  The per-cell protein quantification uses the Xenium cell segmentation labels projected onto the MACSima images. Any residual registration error directly propagates into protein allocation. Cells at the boundary of registration artifacts or at the tissue edge may receive inaccurate protein measurements.  The current computational workflow performs image registration of MACSima images to the Xenium coordinate system. As with any image transformation and resampling procedure, image registration involves interpolation of pixel values. Therefore, minor changes in pixel intensities may occur in the registered images. In our experience, these effects were not observed to materially impact the intended downstream analyses, including RNA-protein based cell annotation and spatial characterization of tissue microenvironments.  The scripts process each TMA core independently. Cross-core normalization of protein signal intensities is not performed automatically and must be applied by the user if comparing protein levels across cores or slides, due to the technical variation within staining intensities. There are several normalization methods (e.g., Y score, ComBat, MxNorm or mean division) that can fail to consider skewed patterns that arise from this type of data. Thus, we recommend using a more reliable non-parametric normalization methods that can be employed in both pixel and feature level, such as UniForm.  30      Troubleshooting   Problem 1: Insufficient quencher removal after Xenium-processing (related to step 12 in the protocol)  Occasionally, incomplete removal of the Xenium autofluorescence quencher using quencher removal solution (10 mM sodium hydrosulfite) may be observed, indicated by persistent lilac discoloration of the tissue section ( Figure 1 ).    Potential solution 
   •  Verify that the sodium hydrosulfite solution was freshly prepared at a final concentration of 10 mM prior to use.    •  If quencher removal was insufficient, repeat this step with freshly prepared quencher removal solution and use it immediately after preparation.   
   Problem 2: Low/insufficient antigen staining intensity (related to before you begin step 8 and step 13 in the protocol)  Xenium-processed slides may exhibit reduced or absent staining for previously established antigen markers during MICS imaging. Compatibility of an antibody clone with standard MACSima workflows does not necessarily guarantee successful staining performance on post-Xenium tissue sections.    Potential solution 
   •  Confirm proper antibody storage conditions and expiration dates, and assess antibody performance using appropriate control tissues.    •  Optimize HIER by extending the incubation time up to 60 min, ensuring that slides remain fully submerged throughout the retrieval process, and testing alternative antigen retrieval buffers (e.g., pH 6).    •  Evaluate alternative antibody clones or, where applicable, fluorescently label validated unlabeled primary immunohistochemistry antibodies to enable compatibility with MICS.    •  We suggest performing a mock Xenium run on a consecutive section to test and optimize antibody clones and establish panels that are suitable for post-Xenium MICS experiments mimicking v1 or 5k panel conditions. Note that the mock experiment should be considered a pre-screening approach rather than a substitute for validation following the complete Xenium workflow.   ○  For the mock Xenium run, mount a serial section (from the same block as the section used for the Xenium-MACSima experiment) onto a blank Xenium slide.   -  Perform sectioning of the block and initial sample preparation comprising deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking as described in steps 1–3.    -  Perform the subsequent steps, including hybridization, post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification, using only the buffer components from previously used  Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000460), but omit the enzymes.    -  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler as described in step 4, using the hybridization mix without a probe panel.    -  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining as described in step 7.    -  Following sample preparation, setup the samples on the Xenium Analyzer according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ) as described in step 8. Prepare all the buffers as mentioned in the above user guide. Decoding reagents are replaced with plates containing 1x PBS. Start the run and define ROIs as mentioned in step 9.    -  After the mock Xenium run is complete, replace the buffer on the slides with 0.05 % PBST and store at 4°C until quencher removal and subsequent MICS imaging (step 12 onwards).       ○  Alternatively, a mock Xenium run can also be performed in an off-the-Xenium-Analyzer setting. In this case, mount the serial section onto a SuperFrost Plus slide. The sample preparation workflow from deparaffinization to nuclei staining is exactly as mentioned above. Following sample preparation, incubate slides in Probe Removal Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C) followed by Wash Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C), at least 4 cycles each, to mimic buffer exposure during the Xenium Analyzer processing. Buffers are prepared as per the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).       •  An antibody should be considered compatible when it fulfills the following criteria (see  Figure 3 ):   ○  Specific staining pattern: Signal is restricted to the expected cell population and subcellular localization.    ○  High signal-to-background ratio: Positive cells are clearly distinguishable from surrounding tissue with minimal nonspecific background.    ○  Reproducible performance: Comparable staining is observed across technical replicates or appropriate control tissues.    ○  Preserved staining after Xenium processing: The staining pattern is consistent with the expected biology, previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation, and comparable to reference databases.       •  The resulting images ( Figure 3 ) allow users to identify antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C, 3D, 3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria.   
   Problem 3: Autofocus failure with large ROIs during MICS (related to step 22 in the protocol)  Selecting tissue sections that cover the entire Xenium imageable area as a single, large ROI during ROI definition on the MACSima instrument occasionally resulted in autofocus instability during imaging. Such issues manifested as blurry FOVs or blurry images in the output folders ( Figure 5 ). In our experience, ROIs larger than approximately 100 FOVs were more prone to the aforementioned focusing issues.    Potential solution 
   •  Divide large imaging areas into smaller ROIs to improve autofocus performance and overall image quality.    •  Select the image contrast-based focusing approach instead of constant height-based focusing for your MICS experiment.    •  Cover the MACSwell frame with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to prevent evaporation and drying of the sample during extended imaging cycles, as insufficient liquid coverage may lead to autofocus and imaging issues.    •  If the tissue to be imaged is larger than the above-mentioned limitation, consider splitting it into several (non-overlapping) ROIs.    •  For TMAs, every core should be imaged as a separate ROI.    •  We suggest using the slides from a mock Xenium run to test suitable ROI sizes and decide on the best autofocusing method.   
   Problem 4: SIFT registration fails or produces identity affine matrix  A failed or bad quality registration could be due to the identification of too few matching keypoints between the Xenium and MACSima DAPI images.    Potential solution  Verify that the correct DAPI file is used (cycle-0 stained DAPI with “_S_” flag, not the baseline “_B_“ image). Try reducing scale_factor from 3 to 2 for higher-resolution feature detection. If images have very low contrast, adjust the CLAHE parameters in preprocess_reg().  21   Confirm that the Xenium morphology focus images contain the expected core region by visually inspecting the cropped image.    Problem 5: Xenium positions do not match MACSima ROI position  If some Xenium positions do not match the MACSima ROI positions, these cores were probably not captured during MACSima scanning (e.g., edge cores or tissue damage).    Potential solution  Do not include these positions in the roi_map_file CSV file, so that they are skipped in the full-slide processing script (“match_rois_cores_fullslide.py”).    Problem 6: Variable registration offset across the tissue  The presence of a misalignment between the Xenium DAPI image and the registered MACSima image that is not constant in magnitude and direction across the image shows that a global affine transformation is insufficient to register the images correctly. A visual inspection of the overlaid Xenium and registered MACSima DAPI image allows for the easy identification of this issue by showing a non-uniform alignment quality across the image. This heterogeneous misalignment is more common for larger ROIs and typically arises from tissue deformation or folding between acquisitions, lens distortion in either imaging system, different tissue mounting geometry, or non-linear shrinkage or expansion of the section.    Potential solution  A non-rigid (deformable) transformation is required.     Note:   Non-rigid (deformable) transformation is not addressed in this protocol, as only a single transformation type was tested. This represents a current limitation; users are advised to adapt the methodology as needed for their specific application. Recommended alternatives are RAMI2D  31   or ST-align.  32       Additional computational problems and diagnostic tips  Other possible computational problems could lead to TMA cores being skipped or output folders not being written due to lack of disk-space ( Table 4 ). For troubleshooting the user can refer to the error message to identify the cause of the problem and correct their workflow or report it as an issue on the GitHub repository associated with this protocol ( https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium ).
